Data Collection & Preprocessing

⏱ 6–12 months 👥 5–10 engineers 💰 $50K–$500K
▼
🌐 Web
📚 Books
🔬 Papers
💬 Forums
Clean Dataset

Imagine you're teaching a child to read. You'd give them millions of books, articles, and conversations. That's exactly what we do — except we collect trillions of words from the internet, books, and research papers. Then we clean it up: remove spam, duplicates, and offensive content.

The corpus must be carefully curated: Common Crawl (petabytes of web data), books corpora (Books1/2), Wikipedia, GitHub, arXiv, StackExchange, etc. Preprocessing includes: deduplication (MinHash/SimHash), quality filtering (perplexity-based), PII redaction, language detection, and document scoring. The Datatrove or Apache Spark pipelines are typical at scale.

📜 Foundational Paper Timeline
2019C4 — Raffel et al. "Exploring the Limits of Transfer Learning" — introduced quality-filtered Common Crawl; colossal-clean-crawled-corpus
2020The Pile — Gao et al. (EleutherAI) — 825GB diverse, high-quality text; first major open research corpus
2022ROOTS / BLOOM — BigScience — multilingual 1.6TB corpus; pioneered data governance & PII filtering at scale
2023RedPajama-1T / Dolma (AI2) — first fully open LLaMA-style training corpora; reproducible pipelines
2024FineWeb-Edu (HuggingFace) — LLM-based quality scoring; 15T tokens; showed educational content quality >> quantity
2024Phi-3 / Nemotron — Synthetic data pipelines; "textbook quality" data generation with LLMs
🔬 Active Research (2024–25)
  • Synthetic data scaling — can LLM-generated data replace web crawls? (Phi series, Nemotron-4)
  • Data mixing laws — Ye et al. showed domain mixture affects loss beyond scale
  • Data attribution — which training examples cause which behaviors? (TRAK, influence functions)
  • Decontamination — detecting benchmark leakage in pretraining corpora
  • Multimodal corpora — interleaved image-text (LAION-5B, OBELICS)
🚀 Open Research Directions
  • Can we train frontier models entirely on synthetic data? At what scale does quality collapse?
  • Optimal data curriculum — should data ordering matter? Evidence is mixed.
  • Continuous web ingestion — training on a live stream without catastrophic forgetting
  • Legal & ethical data sourcing — post-NYT lawsuit era, how do labs license training data?
  • Low-resource languages — most corpora are English-centric; multilingual coverage gaps
📦
Data Volume
Hundreds of billions of words (think 10 million books)
1–10 TB tokens; GPT-3 used 300B tokens, LLaMA-3 used 15T tokens

🏢 Startup Lens — Data Collection
💡 Startup Strategy
  • Don't build your own crawler. Use Common Crawl (free, petabytes) + The Pile + RedPajama. OpenAI and Anthropic both started with publicly available data.
  • Vertical first: If you're building a medical LLM, license PubMed + clinical notes from one health system. Cheaper than general corpus and differentiates you.
  • Legal risk is real. Post-NYT lawsuit, document every source. Use AI2's open-licensed Dolma or EleutherAI's The Pile to stay safe.
  • Budget reality: A 7B-param startup can pre-train on FineWeb-Edu (free, 15T tokens) + 2 data engineers + 3 months = <$50K before compute.
💰 Startup Cost Reality
DIY crawler (team + infra)$200K–$800K
License existing corpus$10K–$100K
Open-source data only$0 + engineer time
Synthetic data (GPT-4 API)$5K–$50K
💡 Founder tip: Mistral, Phi, and Falcon all used mostly open-source data. Your moat is curation quality and domain focus — not crawling more of the internet.
👤 First Hire for This Stage
Senior Data Engineer
One great data engineer beats three average ones. Find someone who has worked on ML data pipelines at scale (not just regular ETL).
Where to find: ex-Hugging Face, ex-EleutherAI, ML Twitter/X community, Papers With Code contributors
Comp: $180K–$250K + 0.5–1.5% equity (seed stage)
💰 Investor Lens — Data Collection
📊 Cost Structure
  • DIY web crawler team + infra: $200K–$800K
  • Licensing curated corpus: $10K–$500K/yr
  • Synthetic data (API costs): $5K–$100K
  • Human annotation labor: $50K–$2M
  • Storage & compute for preprocessing: $20K–$200K
🏰 What Makes a Data Moat
  • Proprietary real-world data (clinical records, legal docs, code repos)
  • Exclusive licensing agreements with data owners
  • Continuously updated live data pipelines
  • Domain-specific annotation by subject matter experts
  • Data flywheels: user interactions improve the model which attracts more users
🚩 Investor Red Flags
  • Unlicensed scraping of copyrighted content (NYT lawsuit risk)
  • No data provenance or lineage tracking
  • 100% dependency on one data supplier
  • PII in training data without consent mechanisms
  • No data audit trail for regulatory compliance
🔍 Due Diligence Questions
  • What licenses cover your training data?
  • Can a competitor replicate your dataset in 12 months?
  • What's your cost per million clean tokens?
  • How do you handle data that goes stale?
  • What's your GDPR/CCPA compliance posture?
💡 Investor insight: Data is the highest-leverage asset in AI. A company with 10x better data and 1x the model will beat a company with 1x data and 10x the model. Prioritize data defensibility over model novelty at early stages.
🧭 Founder Lens — Data Collection
🔍 Gaps Nobody Is Filling
  • Non-English web data — 50+ languages have near-zero high-quality training corpora. The next frontier model for Swahili, Tamil, or Tagalog is open for the taking.
  • Multimodal real-world data — sensor data, industrial IoT streams, agricultural telemetry. Completely untapped for LLM training.
  • Long-context professional documents — legal case law, medical research, engineering specs. No one has done this at scale.
  • Procedural how-to data — step-by-step workflows, technical manuals, repair guides. Massive demand, almost no good training sets.
💡 Differentiation Strategy
  • Own a vertical's data. If you exclusively license clinical trial data from 500 hospitals, no one can replicate your medical LLM without that partnership.
  • Build the data flywheel early. Every user interaction is training data. Design your product to generate the data your next model needs.
  • Data quality over quantity. Phi-3 by Microsoft outperformed models 5x its size using curated "textbook quality" data. This is the arbitrage.
  • Synthetic data generation. Use GPT-4 to bootstrap training data for your niche — few startups are doing this systematically yet.
🚀 Founder Action
  • Before writing a line of code, spend 3 months interviewing 50 domain experts about their data pain points
  • Sign your first data partnership agreement before raising a single dollar
  • Build a data advisory board with 3–5 domain expert insiders who can open doors
🧭 Founder principle: Your data strategy IS your company strategy. The founders who win in 2026 will be those who secured unique data access in 2024–25 when nobody was paying attention.
⚡ Agentic Lens — Data Collection
🕷️ Agentic Crawlers

Traditional data pipelines are static — fixed URLs, scheduled downloads. Agentic data collection uses browser-driving agents that navigate websites like humans: filling forms, following pagination, handling login walls, adapting to UI changes without re-engineering. GPT-4o + Playwright agents at Llama 3's data team collected 3× more diverse web content than script-based crawlers.

🎯 Active Learning Agents

Instead of scraping everything and filtering later, active learning agents identify which data would most improve model performance and selectively collect it. An agent monitors model weaknesses, generates targeted queries, finds relevant sources, and adds only the high-signal data — reducing collection cost by 60-80% while improving final model quality.

✅ Quality Assessment Agents

Autonomous agents evaluate data quality at ingestion time: detecting near-duplicates, flagging low-quality text, identifying potential copyright issues, and scoring educational value (phi-2 "textbook quality" methodology). What previously needed human review teams now runs continuously at petabyte scale.

⚡ Agentic data pipelines are now standard at frontier labs — the data flywheel that feeds the model is itself an agentic system, making data collection a competitive moat that compounds over time.
💰 Investor Lens — Data Collection
CapEx Reality
  • Total data stage cost: $200K–$2M depending on proprietary vs open-source mix
  • DIY web crawl: $500K–$2M (team + storage + bandwidth)
  • Open-source only path: $50K–$200K (engineering time, cloud storage)
  • Domain-specific licensing (medical, legal, financial): $100K–$1M/year
  • Key metric investors track: tokens per dollar — efficiency of data acquisition
Data Moat Assessment
  • Proprietary data = durable competitive advantage — hardest thing for competitors to replicate
  • Exclusive data licensing agreements: how long? Renewal terms? Exclusivity clauses?
  • Synthetic data: can LLMs generate training data indefinitely? Quality ceiling unknown
  • Data partnerships (e.g., Reddit–OpenAI $60M/yr deal) are increasingly valuable IP
  • Ask: will this data still be differentiating in 3 years, or will it commoditize?
Red Flags for Investors
  • Unlicensed scraping with no legal review — one NYT-style lawsuit can kill the company
  • No data provenance documentation — impossible to defend in court or due diligence
  • 100% reliance on Common Crawl — no proprietary data = no defensible moat
  • PII in training data — GDPR/CCPA liability; EU AI Act compliance issues
  • Single-source dependency — if that source changes terms, training pipeline breaks
Due Diligence Questions
  • How defensible is your data? Can a competitor replicate it in 12 months?
  • What is your long-term data licensing cost trajectory?
  • Do you have a data governance framework and legal sign-off?
  • What percentage of training data is proprietary vs public?
  • What's your data refresh strategy as knowledge cutoffs become competitive?
💡 Investor insight: The best AI companies own data others can't access. A proprietary data moat compounds over time — every new customer interaction feeds the training loop, widening the gap from competitors who rely on static public datasets.

Tokenization

⏱ 1–2 months 👥 1–3 engineers 💰 $5K–$20K
▼
Hello, I love building AI systems!
↓ Tokenizer ↓
Hello, I love building AI systems!
IDs: [15496, 11, 314, 1842, 2615, 9552, 3341, 0]

Computers can't read words — they only understand numbers. Tokenization chops text into small pieces (called tokens) and assigns each a number. "Hello" might become [72, 101, 108, 108, 111] or just [15496] depending on the method. GPT-4 uses about 100,000 different tokens.

Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) or SentencePiece iteratively merges frequent character pairs to form a vocabulary of ~32K–100K subword tokens. The tokenizer is trained on a representative subset of the corpus. Vocabulary size trades off between sequence length (larger vocab = shorter sequences) and embedding table memory. GPT-4 uses cl100k_base (100,277 tokens).

📜 Foundational Paper Timeline
2012WordPiece — Schuster & Nakamura (Google) — subword tokenization for Japanese/Korean; later adopted in BERT
2016BPE for NMT — Sennrich et al. — adapted compression algorithm for NLP; became the dominant method
2018SentencePiece — Kudo & Richardson (Google) — language-agnostic, trains directly on raw text; used in LLaMA
2022tiktoken (OpenAI) — efficient BPE implementation; cl100k_base for GPT-4; byte-level fallback
2023MEGABYTE — Yu et al. (Meta) — tokenizer-free, operates directly on raw bytes with hierarchical model
2024BLT (Byte Latent Transformer) — Meta — dynamic byte patching; matches BPE performance without fixed vocab
🔬 Active Research (2024–25)
  • Tokenizer-free models — BLT shows byte-level can match subword; cheaper inference for non-Latin scripts
  • Tokenization bias — BPE encodes numbers digit-by-digit; hurts arithmetic; studied by Nogueira et al.
  • Vocabulary transfer — can you extend a tokenizer post-hoc? Critical for multilingual adaptation
  • Morphologically-aware tokenization for low-resource languages
🚀 Open Research Directions
  • Is the tokenizer a bottleneck? Can end-to-end learned tokenization outperform BPE?
  • Optimal vocabulary size as a function of model scale — no principled theory yet
  • Tokenization for multimodal — unified discrete tokenizers for text, image, audio (e.g., VQVAE)
  • Can removing tokenization unlock better reasoning? (byte models see individual digits)
🔤
Vocabulary Size
50,000–100,000 unique token types
GPT-2: 50,257 | LLaMA: 32,000 | GPT-4: 100,277
Vocab size ∝ sqrt(corpus size) heuristic; Zouhar et al. 2023 showed optimal vocab minimizes total FLOPs; fertility (tokens/word) matters for non-English
📐
Algorithm
A smart compression algorithm that finds common word pieces
BPE (GPT series), WordPiece (BERT), Unigram LM (SentencePiece)
BPE: greedy frequency merging — deterministic but sub-optimal; Unigram LM: probabilistic, allows stochastic sampling; BLT: content-aware dynamic patching

🏢 Startup Lens — Tokenization
💡 Startup Strategy
  • Don't reinvent the wheel. Use tiktoken (OpenAI, MIT licensed) or SentencePiece directly. Training your own tokenizer only makes sense if you're heavily multilingual or byte-level.
  • Reuse LLaMA's tokenizer if you're building on top of LLaMA-3 family — already trained, tested, 128K vocab, excellent multilingual coverage.
  • This stage costs almost nothing at startup scale. One engineer, one week. Don't over-invest.
  • Exception: Domain-specific vocab (genomics, legal, medical codes) may warrant custom token merges — worth 2 weeks of ablation.
💰 Cost Reality
Reuse existing (tiktoken/SP)~$0
Train custom BPE from scratch$2K–$10K
Full tokenise corpus (compute)$5K–$30K
💡 Founder tip: Spending engineering time here is opportunity cost from pre-training. Adopt and adapt — validate your choice with fertility stats in a day, then move on.
💰 Investor Lens — Tokenization
📊 Cost & Investment Reality
  • One-time engineering cost: $5K–$50K
  • Usually 1–2 senior engineers for 2–4 weeks
  • Lowest CapEx stage in the entire pipeline
  • Open-source tokenizers (tiktoken, SentencePiece) = near-zero cost
  • Custom tokenizer: only justified for niche language domains
💎 Underestimated Value Driver
  • Tokenizer quality directly impacts model efficiency and quality
  • Multilingual tokenizer coverage = bigger addressable market (TAM)
  • Code-optimized tokenizers unlock developer market ($50B+ TAM)
  • Better tokenization = shorter sequences = lower inference cost = better margins
  • Tokenizer IP can be separately licensed in enterprise deals
🔍 Investor Signals to Watch
  • Does the company measure and optimize fertility rate?
  • Do they benchmark tokenization speed at inference scale?
  • Have they thought about tokenizer upgrades without breaking existing APIs?
  • Is tokenizer versioning part of their model governance?
💡 Investor insight: Tokenization is low-cost but high-impact. A 10% improvement in tokenizer efficiency at 1B tokens/day of inference translates to millions in annual compute savings. Ask founders if they've measured this.
🧭 Founder Lens — Tokenization
💡 Unseen Opportunity
  • Domain-specific tokenizers for code, math, chemistry, genomics — current tokenizers handle these poorly. A tokenizer optimized for SMILES notation (chemistry) is 40% more efficient than tiktoken.
  • Lossless compression as a moat — better tokenization = shorter sequences = 30% cheaper inference = pricing power over OpenAI.
  • Multilingual-first tokenizer for ASEAN, African, or Middle Eastern languages — still near-zero competition in 2025.
🔍 Founder Strategy
  • Don't build a general-purpose tokenizer — you can't out-resource OpenAI. Own a specific domain where their tokenizer is provably worse.
  • Publish your tokenizer as open-source to build credibility and community before monetizing. Hugging Face won by giving away the tools.
  • Benchmark your tokenizer against tiktoken on your domain and publish the numbers — this is your credibility in the research community.
🧭 Founder principle: The best founders see tokenization not as a technical step but as a product decision. How you tokenize defines what your model can express. Own the representation layer in your domain.
⚡ Agentic Lens — Preprocessing
🔍 Agentic Data Auditing

Preprocessing agents sample batches, run quality metrics (perplexity, deduplication ratio, toxicity scores), identify systematic issues (encoding errors, non-native language contamination, benchmark data leakage), and generate automated reports with fix recommendations — replacing weeks of manual data curation per training run.

🔄 Synthetic Data Agents

When real data is scarce or low quality, agents generate synthetic training examples. GPT-4 generates math reasoning chains; Claude generates diverse instruction-following samples; coding agents generate test cases and solutions. Models like Phi-3 and Orca were trained substantially on GPT-4-generated synthetic data — the student surpasses the teacher.

⚖️ Deduplication & Balancing

Minhash LSH deduplication agents identify near-duplicate documents at trillion-token scale without human review. Separate agents analyze domain distribution, detect over-represented sources (Common Crawl bias), and rebalance the dataset to Chinchilla-optimal composition — tasks that previously required months of data science work.

⚡ The best preprocessing pipelines today are themselves LLM-powered — using smaller models to filter data for larger models, creating a recursive quality improvement loop.
💰 Investor Lens — Tokenization
Cost Profile
  • Total tokenization spend: typically $5K–$50K — the cheapest stage
  • Reusing open-source tokenizers: near-zero cost beyond 1–2 weeks of engineering
  • Custom domain tokenizer (medical codes, genomics): $10K–$50K in compute + time
  • Corpus tokenization at 15T tokens: ~$5K–$30K in cloud compute
  • Often overlooked in due diligence — but decisions here lock in for years
TAM Implications
  • Multilingual tokenizer coverage = access to non-English markets = bigger TAM
  • Poor CJK/Arabic tokenization: 3–5× more tokens per character → 3–5× higher inference cost for those users
  • Tokenizer fertility directly affects cost per query in non-Latin scripts
  • European AI regulation (EU AI Act) increasingly scrutinizes multilingual fairness
  • Ask: does the tokenizer support the company's international expansion roadmap?
Quality Signal
  • Tokenizer quality silently affects every downstream capability and revenue metric
  • Poor number tokenization → poor arithmetic → reduced enterprise use cases
  • Sub-optimal vocabulary size → longer sequences → higher inference cost → lower margins
  • Red flag: team that hasn't measured "fertility" metrics across target domains
  • Green flag: team that A/B tested 3+ tokenizer configs and can explain the choice
💡 Investor insight: Tokenizer decisions made in week two of a startup are still costing (or saving) money three years later on every inference request. A 20% improvement in tokenization efficiency compounds across billions of API calls — it's one of the highest-leverage, lowest-cost decisions in the entire stack.

Model Architecture Design

⏱ 2–6 months 👥 3–8 researchers 💰 $100K–$500K
▼
Token + Position Embedding
Multi-Head Attention 🔍
Feed-Forward Network ⚡
Multi-Head Attention 🔍
Feed-Forward Network ⚡
Multi-Head Attention 🔍
Feed-Forward Network ⚡
· · · (96 more layers) · · ·
Output: Probability over Vocabulary

Now we design the AI's "brain". The most important invention here is called Attention — it lets the AI focus on the right words when making predictions, just like how you focus on key words when reading a sentence. We stack many layers of these attention blocks on top of each other.

The decoder-only transformer (GPT architecture) consists of L stacked blocks, each containing: multi-head causal self-attention (Q/K/V projections), followed by a position-wise FFN (typically 4× hidden dim with GELU/SwiGLU). Key design choices: RoPE vs ALiBi positional encodings, GQA vs MHA, RMSNorm vs LayerNorm, context length, and MoE vs dense FFN.

📜 Architecture Evolution Timeline
2017Attention Is All You Need — Vaswani et al. (Google) — transformer architecture; multi-head attention; positional encoding; still the backbone today
2018GPT-1 — Radford et al. (OpenAI) — decoder-only transformer for generative LM; 117M params; introduced the pretraining paradigm
2020GPT-3 — Brown et al. — 175B params; showed in-context learning; few-shot prompting without gradient updates
2022PaLM — Chowdhery et al. (Google) — 540B; Pathways system; SwiGLU FFN; parallel attention+FFN; MQA
2022FlashAttention — Dao et al. — IO-aware exact attention; 2–4× speedup; enabled longer contexts economically
2023LLaMA-2 — Touvron et al. (Meta) — GQA, RoPE, SwiGLU; open weights; became the research community's reference model
2023Mamba — Gu & Dao — Selective State Space Model (SSM); linear complexity; competitive with transformers on many tasks
2024Jamba (AI21), Zamba — hybrid transformer+Mamba architectures; best of both worlds
🔬 Active Research (2024–25)
  • Sub-quadratic attention — linear attention (RetNet, RWKV), SSMs (Mamba-2), hybrid models
  • Long context — LLaMA-3.1 1M tokens via RoPE scaling; YaRN, LongLoRA, LongRoPE
  • Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) — Mixtral 8×7B, DeepSeek-MoE; 8 experts, route 2 per token; 4× efficiency
  • Multimodal architectures — LLaVA, Gemini, Flamingo; visual/audio token integration
  • Architecture search — scaling laws for layer depth vs width (Hu et al. 2024)
🚀 Open Research Directions
  • Can SSMs (Mamba) match transformers at scale? Evidence so far mixed at 70B+
  • Truly unbounded context — current long-context is still approximate or expensive
  • Weight sharing and modularity — can we reuse sub-networks across tasks?
  • Mechanistic understanding — what do attention heads actually compute? (Elhage et al., circuits work)

💰 Investor Lens — Model Architecture
📊 R&D Burn Rate
  • Research team salaries: $1M–$5M/yr (5–10 PhDs)
  • Ablation experiments (small compute): $100K–$500K
  • Architecture search & prototyping: $200K–$1M
  • No product revenue during this phase — pure R&D burn
  • Investors fund this as a bet on the team's technical taste
🏆 IP & Competitive Moat
  • Novel architecture = patentable (e.g., Mixture of Experts, Flash Attention)
  • Efficiency gains → lower inference cost → higher gross margin
  • Architecture choices compound: hard to change after pre-training
  • SSMs (Mamba), sparse attention, sub-quadratic methods = cost moats
  • Published architecture papers attract top researcher talent
🚩 Risk Flags
  • Team stuck in research mode — won't ship a product
  • Architecture too novel = longer de-risking timeline
  • No ablation evidence that novel design actually helps
  • Overfitting to one benchmark that doesn't reflect product use
  • Key researcher departure = architecture knowledge risk
🔍 Due Diligence Questions
  • What's your FLOPs/parameter efficiency vs GPT-4/LLaMA-3?
  • Can your architecture scale to 100B+ parameters without redesign?
  • What hardware does your architecture optimize for?
  • How long until you have a working prototype at small scale?
💡 Investor insight: Architecture is where technical founders often over-invest. The best architectures are often the simplest. Anthropic and OpenAI both use transformer variants, not exotic designs. Bet on the team's judgment, not novelty for its own sake.
🧭 Founder Lens — Architecture
🔮 Architecture Bets Nobody Is Making (2025–26)
  • Hybrid SSM-Transformer models (Mamba + attention) — 10x better on long contexts, but very few startups are commercializing this.
  • On-device / edge LLMs — sub-1B parameter models that run on phones. Apple Silicon + Qualcomm NPUs make this suddenly feasible. Massive untapped market.
  • Mixture-of-Experts for verticals — domain-specific expert routing. No one has done MoE for healthcare or legal specifically.
  • Neuromorphic / energy-efficient architectures — as data center power becomes the bottleneck, efficiency architectures will be worth billions.
  • Multimodal architectures for industrial IoT — text + sensor + video for manufacturing. No frontier lab is focused here.
🧭 When to Be Bold, When to Be Boring
  • Be bold on architecture when you have a unique insight backed by early experimental evidence.
  • Be boring (use transformers) when you need to ship a product in 12 months and can't afford 18 months of architecture research.
  • The graveyard of AI startups is full of companies that spent 2 years on novel architecture and ran out of money before shipping.
  • Publish architecture papers early — this builds credibility, attracts researchers, and is free marketing.
🚀 Differentiation Framework
  • Can OpenAI replicate your architecture bet in 6 months? If yes, find a different bet.
  • Does your architecture unlock a use case that's currently impossible? That's a defensible moat.
  • Is there a PhD who published the key paper you're building on? Hire them. They're your technical credibility.
🧭 Founder principle: The architecture is a bet on the future. Make the bet deliberately, not by default. The founders who win make architecture choices that enable their business model, not architecture choices that look impressive in papers.
⚡ Agentic Lens — Architecture Design
🧬 Neural Architecture Search Agents

NAS agents explore architecture hyperparameter spaces (attention heads, layer depth, FFN ratio, activation functions) by training proxy models, evaluating them, and iteratively refining the search — automating what previously required domain experts. Google's Gemini and Apple's on-device models used NAS agents to find efficiency-optimized architectures.

🔬 Ablation Automation

Agents design and run ablation studies autonomously: vary one component, hold others constant, measure impact, log results, generate hypothesis about why performance changed, design the next experiment. What took a research team weeks of coordination now runs as an overnight automated pipeline — compressing architecture iteration cycles from months to days.

📐 Architecture Code Generation

Coding agents (Claude Code, Copilot) now write architecture implementations from spec — translating a paper's pseudocode into production-ready PyTorch/JAX, including custom CUDA kernels for attention variants. The time to implement a novel architecture dropped from 2-4 weeks to 1-3 days for a skilled team using AI coding agents.

⚡ Architecture design is shifting from human intuition to agent-assisted search — the best architectures in 2026 (MLA, sliding window, MoE variants) were discovered through automated exploration that no human team could run manually at the same speed.
📦 Handoff to Next Stage
Delivers: model code (GitHub repo, reviewed & tested), architecture design doc, hyperparameter starting points, MFU benchmarks on small scale → Pre-Training team
🏢 Startup Lens — Architecture
💡 Startup Strategy
  • Start from open weights, not scratch. Mistral 7B, LLaMA-3 8B, Falcon — all MIT/Llama licensed. Continuing pre-training on an open base saves 80% of compute vs from scratch.
  • Vertical beats general. A 7B model fine-tuned on legal data beats GPT-3.5-level for legal tasks. You can't out-scale OpenAI — so out-specialise them.
  • Pick your differentiating architectural bet. Mistral bet on sliding window attention. Mamba bets on SSMs. What is your 18-month bet? Long context? Multimodal? Reasoning?
  • Run architecture ablations at 1B scale before committing to a 70B run. Every architectural decision costs 10× more to change later.

  • Ablation experiments at 1B scale: $10K–$100K per round of experiments

💡 Investor insight: Architectural novelty is the hardest thing to evaluate in an AI investment but one of the most valuable. A team that designed Mixtral's MoE routing or DeepSeek's Multi-head Latent Attention has compounding technical capital — those insights speed every future training run.

Pre-Training

⏱ 3–18 months 👥 5–20 engineers 💰 $1M–$100M+
▼
GPU
GPU

GPU

GPU
GPU
GPU

This is the most expensive step. We feed the model all our data and make it predict the next word billions of times. Every time it's wrong, we adjust its internal numbers slightly. After doing this trillions of times across thousands of powerful GPUs running for months, the model learns to predict language incredibly well.

Pre-training is autoregressive next-token prediction minimizing cross-entropy loss via AdamW optimizer with cosine LR scheduling and warmup. Requires distributed training: tensor parallelism, pipeline parallelism, and data parallelism (3D parallelism). Megatron-LM, DeepSpeed ZeRO, or FSDP are standard frameworks. Chinchilla scaling laws guide optimal token/parameter ratios (≈20 tokens per parameter).

📜 Scaling & Training Timeline
2020Scaling Laws — Kaplan et al. (OpenAI) — power law relationships: L ∝ N⁻⁰·⁰⁷⁶, L ∝ D⁻⁰·⁰⁹⁵; guided GPT-3 design
2021Megatron-LM v2 — Narayanan et al. — 3D parallelism (tensor+pipeline+data); trained 1T params; enabled modern scale
2022Chinchilla — Hoffmann et al. (DeepMind) — revised scaling laws; optimal: equal scaling of params & tokens; invalidated GPT-3 training ratio
2022DeepSpeed ZeRO-3 — Rajbhandari et al. (Microsoft) — shards optimizer states/gradients/params; 10× memory reduction
2023LLaMA — Touvron et al. — trained 65B on 1.4T tokens (over-trained vs Chinchilla); showed inference-optimal ≠ training-optimal
2024MuP (Maximal Update Parameterization) — Yang et al. — hyperparameter transfer across scales; tune at small scale, apply at large scale
🔬 Active Research (2024–25)
  • Over-training vs Chinchilla-optimal — LLaMA showed inference-optimal models need more tokens than Chinchilla suggests
  • Curriculum learning — does data ordering matter? Blevins et al. showed domain ordering helps math/code
  • Continual pretraining — adding new knowledge post-training without catastrophic forgetting (DARE, TIES merging)
  • Training instabilities — loss spikes at scale; μP helps but doesn't eliminate; relationship to learning rate warmup
  • Compute-optimal frontier — DeepSeek-V2 showed MoE changes the Pareto frontier significantly
🚀 Open Research Directions
  • Do scaling laws hold past 10²⁸ FLOPs? Extrapolation is uncertain; wall may exist
  • Alternative training objectives beyond next-token prediction — masked diffusion, MDLM
  • Online/streaming training on live data without full retraining
  • Hardware-aware architecture co-design — training cost depends heavily on memory bandwidth
  • Understanding loss spikes — no consensus on cause; critical for reliable long runs

💰 Investor Lens — Pre-training
📊 The CapEx Reality
  • 1B param model on 50B tokens: ~$50K–$200K
  • 7B param model on 1T tokens: ~$500K–$2M

⚠️ Investor Scrutiny Points
  • Compute cost is the single biggest risk item on the cap table
  • Cost per FLOP declining ~2.5x/yr — timing the training run matters
  • Training failures (loss spikes, divergence) = wasted capital
  • No early stopping metrics = burning money blind
  • Cloud vs owned hardware: cloud flexibility vs long-term margin
💡 Efficiency = Competitive Advantage
  • Chinchilla-optimal training = best model for your compute budget
  • MFU (Model FLOP Utilization) >50% = excellent engineering
  • Distributed training expertise is rare and highly valuable
  • Mistral trained GPT-3-class models for 100x less — this is the moat
  • Compute efficiency directly translates to gross margin at inference
🔍 Key Investor Metrics
  • Cost per trillion tokens trained
  • GPU utilization rate during training runs
  • Loss curve trajectory vs published baselines
  • Estimated inference cost per 1M tokens post-training
  • Time-to-first-model: how long from funding to working model?
💡 Investor insight: Pre-training is the biggest single capital allocation decision a frontier AI startup makes. A successful $20M training run creates an asset worth 10–100x more. A failed run loses it all. Investors should ask: what are your failure modes and how do you detect them early?
🧭 Founder Lens — Pre-training
💡 The Efficiency Arbitrage
  • Mistral trained a GPT-4-class model for $5M that cost OpenAI $100M+. The gap was engineering efficiency and Chinchilla-optimal training. This opportunity exists in every domain.
  • Continual pre-training on domain data costs 10–100x less than training from scratch. Startups that find the right base model and adapt it will win verticals against general-purpose labs.
  • Data curation > data volume. The Phi-3 mini (3.8B params) outperformed GPT-3.5 on most benchmarks using curated textbooks. Founders who understand this compound their advantage.
🎯 Founder Decision Framework
  • Train from scratch only if: you have truly unique data that no base model has seen, you have $10M+ compute budget, and you have ex-frontier lab training engineers on the team.
  • Fine-tune instead if: your domain is well-represented in existing base models, you have <$2M compute budget, or your timeline is <12 months to product.
  • Never start a training run without a loss monitoring system, automatic checkpoint saving, and a clear abort criterion. Failed training runs kill startups.
🧠 What Nobody Tells Founders
  • Your first training run will fail. Budget for 2–3 iterations.
  • Hire one "training infrastructure" engineer before anything else — they save you millions in wasted compute.
  • The moment your loss curve diverges is the most stressful day of a founder's life. Have your abort/restart protocol written before you start.
  • Publish your training recipe as a paper — it costs nothing and attracts the best engineers to your team.
🧭 Founder principle: The pre-training decision determines your cost structure for the next 5 years. Founders who find an efficient path to a great base model will have structural margin advantages that accumulate. Think compute ROI, not compute prestige.
⚡ Agentic Lens — Pre-training
🖥️ Training Run Agents

Distributed training at scale (10,000+ GPUs) requires constant monitoring — detecting GPU failures, loss spikes, gradient explosions, and dead nodes. Agentic monitoring systems watch training metrics in real-time, automatically restart failed nodes, checkpoint on anomalies, and page engineers only when human judgment is needed. Meta's OAM (Open Agent Monitoring) reduced manual intervention by 70% during LLaMA 3 training.

⚙️ Hyperparameter Optimization

Bayesian optimization agents (Optuna, Ray Tune) run thousands of small-scale experiments to find optimal learning rate schedules, warmup periods, batch sizes, and gradient clipping thresholds — then extrapolate to full-scale training. These agents replaced the "loss curve intuition" that previously resided exclusively in senior ML engineers.

♻️ Curriculum Learning Agents

Instead of shuffling all data uniformly, curriculum agents order training examples by difficulty — starting simple, introducing hard examples as the model matures. Dynamic curriculum agents monitor model performance on a held-out validation set and continuously adjust the data mix in real-time, converging 15-30% faster than random ordering.

⚡ The single biggest leverage point for agentic pre-training: agents monitoring other agents monitoring GPUs. Automated infrastructure dramatically reduces the senior ML engineer hours required per training run — the bottleneck shifts from "we don't have enough engineers" to "we don't have enough compute."

🏢 Startup Lens — Pre-Training (The Funding Crunch)
💡 Startup Strategy
  • Cloud credits are your lifeline. Apply for AWS Activate ($100K), GCP Startups ($200K), Microsoft for Startups ($150K), and CoreWeave/Lambda Labs startup programs. Stack them.
  • Strategic cloud partnerships. Microsoft invested $13B in OpenAI partly in exchange for Azure compute credits. Google invested in Anthropic for GCP access. Your Series A/B investor may BE your cloud provider.
  • Right-size your run. Train a 7B model on 1T tokens = ~$500K compute. Train a 70B on 2T tokens = ~$5M. Match your training budget to your funding stage.
  • Spot instances cut cost 60–70%. Design your training to be preemption-tolerant (checkpoint every 30 min). Lambda Labs and CoreWeave are 40–60% cheaper than AWS for GPU clusters.
  • Don't train if you don't need to. Many successful AI startups (Cursor, Harvey, Perplexity) built $1B+ businesses on fine-tuned APIs before touching pre-training.
💰 Funding Stage vs Compute Budget
Pre-seed / Friends & FamilyUse cloud credits only. Fine-tune open models.

Series B+ ($100M+)100B+ scale. Negotiate dedicated GPU cluster. Consider owned hardware (H100 at $30K each).

Cloud RentCoreWeave / Lambda Labs / AWS: flexible, no upfront. Best for <$5M runs.

The Biggest CapEx Item

Compute Efficiency Scrutiny

Gross Margin Foundation

  • Model refresh cycles: every 12–18 months for frontier labs = recurring CapEx
  • Investor question: what is your amortized compute cost per 1M inference tokens?
Key Due Diligence Questions
  • What is your compute cost per token at 7B, 70B, and 400B scale?

  • How often will you need to retrain, and what is the expected cost of each run?
💡 Investor insight: Pre-training is where capital intensity determines who can compete. Labs that train more efficiently — higher MFU, better data quality, smarter architectures — will have structurally lower costs and thus higher gross margins than peers spending the same money. This stage is where the moat is built or isn't.

Fine-Tuning (SFT)

⏱ 1–3 months 👥 3–10 people 💰 $50K–$2M
▼
Human:
Explain gravity to me
→
Assistant:
Gravity is the force that pulls objects toward each other. The more massive an object...
📝 Human writes examples
↓
🤖 Model learns style
↓
✅ Model follows instructions

After pre-training, the model can predict text but doesn't know how to be helpful. Fine-tuning is like teaching it manners. We show it thousands of examples of good conversations — "Human asks X, Assistant answers Y" — and it learns to be a helpful assistant instead of just a text predictor.

Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) trains the model on curated instruction-response pairs (FLAN, Alpaca, ShareGPT, OpenAssistant-style data). The base model is fine-tuned on these with a lower LR and fewer steps. Parameter-efficient alternatives: LoRA/QLoRA adapt only a small adapter matrix (r=8–64), reducing trainable params by 99%+ while retaining most of the base model's knowledge.

📜 Instruction Tuning & PEFT Timeline
2021FLAN — Wei et al. (Google) — instruction tuning on 60+ NLP tasks; showed fine-tuning on task descriptions improves zero-shot generalization
2021LoRA — Hu et al. (Microsoft) — low-rank adaptation; freeze base model, train two small matrices (A,B); r×d params instead of d²
2022InstructGPT — Ouyang et al. (OpenAI) — SFT on 13K human-written examples → RLHF; showed alignment via imitation + feedback
2023Alpaca / Self-Instruct — Wang et al. — LLM-generated instruction data (52K examples from text-davinci-003); opened low-cost SFT era
2023QLoRA — Dettmers et al. — 4-bit quantized base + BF16 LoRA adapters; fine-tune 65B on a single 48GB GPU
2024LIMA — Zhou et al. (Meta) — 1000 carefully curated examples ≈ 52K random examples; "less is more" for alignment
🔬 Active Research (2024–25)
  • Synthetic SFT data at scale — Magpie, Nemotron-4 generate millions of instruction pairs autonomously
  • Data quality vs quantity — LIMA showed 1K curated examples can rival much larger datasets
  • Multimodal SFT — LLaVA-style visual instruction tuning; video, audio extensions
  • Code SFT — CodeLLaMA, DeepSeekCoder; code data improves general reasoning
  • Continual SFT — adding new skills without forgetting previous ones (catastrophic forgetting)
🚀 Open Research Directions
  • What makes SFT data "high quality"? No principled definition; IFD score, perplexity filtering are proxies
  • Self-play fine-tuning — can models improve by generating and self-evaluating their own examples?
  • Merge of SFT adapters — model merging (TIES, DARE) to combine domain experts without full retraining
  • When does SFT hurt? Evidence of "alignment tax" on some capabilities; tradeoffs not fully understood
📋
Data Needed
10,000–100,000 human-written Q&A examples
10K–500K instruction pairs; quality > quantity; InstructGPT used ~13K samples

🧭 Founder Lens — Alignment & RLHF
💡 The Alignment Opportunity Founders Miss
  • Domain-aligned models outperform general aligned models in every enterprise vertical. A legally-aligned model that understands privilege and confidentiality is worth 10x a generic assistant to a law firm.
  • Alignment for safety-critical domains (medical, aviation, nuclear) is almost completely unaddressed. Regulatory moat + premium pricing + near-zero competition = founder opportunity of the decade.
  • Cultural alignment — models that genuinely understand cultural nuance for MENA, East Asia, or South Asia markets. Western-aligned models fail badly here.
  • Constitution AI for your domain — write your own constitutional principles for your vertical. This is defensible IP that general-purpose labs can't easily replicate.
🧭 Founder Strategy
  • Don't compete with OpenAI on general alignment. You can't out-resource them. Own alignment for a specific professional domain.
  • Your best alignment data comes from your domain experts — hire 3 senior domain practitioners to review outputs before any annotation team.
  • Alignment = product quality. Every 10% improvement in alignment translates to lower churn and higher NPS. Measure it like a product metric, not a research metric.
  • Build an internal red-team of 5–10 people in your domain who adversarially test your model weekly. This is your early warning system.
🧭 Founder principle: General alignment is a solved (enough) problem at the product level. Domain-specific alignment is completely open. The founder who creates the best-aligned model for oncology, contract law, or aerospace engineering wins that entire vertical.
⚡ Agentic Lens — RLHF & Alignment
🤖 Automated Preference Collection

Constitutional AI (Anthropic) uses an agent to critique and revise model outputs against a written constitution — replacing thousands of human preference labels with automated self-critique. RLAIF (RL from AI Feedback) extends this: a strong model generates preference labels for a weaker model. DeepSeek R1 trained primarily on AI-generated preference data, dramatically reducing human labeler cost.

🔴 Agentic Red Teaming

Red-teaming agents systematically probe models for safety failures — generating thousands of adversarial prompts, jailbreak attempts, and harmful requests automatically. Automated red-teaming finds failure modes 10-50× faster than human red teams and runs continuously as the model evolves, catching regressions before deployment.

🏆 Process Reward Models

PRM agents evaluate not just final answers but each step of reasoning — identifying exactly where in a chain-of-thought the model went wrong. Training with PRM feedback produces models that reason more reliably and correct their own mistakes mid-generation. o1, o3, and R1 all use PRM-based training as their core alignment innovation.

⚡ The key insight: alignment itself is becoming agentic. The model critiques itself, flags its own failures, and generates its own training signal. Human oversight shifts from "label every example" to "define the constitution and validate the automated process."

RLHF — Learning from Human Feedback

⏱ 2–6 months 👥 5–15 people 💰 $200K–$5M
▼
Response A ✅
"Gravity pulls objects..."
Response B ❌
"Gravity is a myth..."
👤 Human ranks A > B
🏅 Reward Model trained
↓
🔄 LLM updated via PPO/DPO

We ask humans to rate two AI responses: "Which is better, A or B?" We collect thousands of these ratings, train a Judge AI on them, then use that judge to continuously improve our main model. This is how ChatGPT learned to sound so natural and helpful — it's basically teaching the AI using human preferences.

RLHF (InstructGPT/ChatGPT approach): (1) Train a Reward Model on human preference pairs (Bradley-Terry model), (2) Fine-tune the policy via PPO with KL-divergence penalty to prevent reward hacking. Modern alternatives: DPO (Direct Preference Optimization) eliminates the separate RM and optimizes preferences directly. GRPO (DeepSeek), RLAIF (Constitutional AI), and SimPO are further refinements.

📜 Alignment & RLHF Timeline
2017Learning from Human Preferences — Christiano et al. (OpenAI) — original RLHF on Atari; foundation of the modern approach
2022InstructGPT — Ouyang et al. (OpenAI) — RLHF on language models at scale; humans preferred InstructGPT 175B over GPT-3 175B
2022Constitutional AI — Bai et al. (Anthropic) — RLAIF; LLM critiques its own outputs using a "constitution"; reduces human annotation
2023DPO — Rafailov et al. (Stanford) — implicit reward; optimizes Bradley-Terry loss directly on policy; no separate RM or PPO
2024GRPO — Shao et al. (DeepSeek) — Group Relative Policy Optimization; removes value model; used in DeepSeek-R1 reasoning model
2024Process Reward Models — Lightman et al. (OpenAI) — reward at each reasoning step, not just final answer; enables o1-style thinking
2024SimPO — Meng et al. — reference-free DPO variant; length-normalized; simpler and competitive
🔬 Active Research (2024–25)
  • Process Reward Models (PRMs) — step-level credit assignment for reasoning; ORM vs PRM debate
  • RLVR (RL from Verifiable Rewards) — DeepSeek-R1; train on math/code with ground-truth reward; no human labels
  • Scalable oversight — can weak supervisors guide stronger models? (Burns et al., Superalignment team)
  • Reward hacking — models overfit reward model; goodhart's law at scale; Coste et al. 2023
  • Constitutional AI scaling — RLAIF can reduce human label cost by 10×; Claude's approach
🚀 Open Research Directions
  • Weak-to-strong generalization — can GPT-4 be supervised by GPT-2-level labels? (OpenAI Superalignment)
  • Debate as alignment — AI models debate; humans judge; can this scale where human evaluation fails?
  • Value alignment vs capability — are safety and capability actually in conflict?
  • Multi-objective alignment — helpfulness, harmlessness, honesty are often in tension; formal treatment lacking
  • Self-improvement loops — can models improve alignment through self-play without human labels?

🧭 Founder Lens — Evaluation
💡 Own the Benchmark in Your Domain
  • Create the eval, own the narrative. Whoever defines what "good" means in a domain sets the standard everyone else chases. HumanEval defined code quality; who defines legal reasoning quality? Medical diagnostic quality? That's open.
  • Publish a domain-specific benchmark as a research paper. This positions you as the authority, attracts researchers, generates citations, and creates the scorecard buyers use when choosing between vendors.
  • Leaderboards are free marketing. If you run the leaderboard for clinical LLMs, you're the center of the ecosystem. Every competitor has to engage with you on your terms.
🧭 Founder Differentiation
  • Your eval framework should measure what your customers actually care about, not academic benchmarks. Talk to 20 customers and ask: "What would convince you this model is good enough to trust with real work?"
  • Build a public eval dashboard your customers can use to verify your claims themselves. Radical transparency builds enterprise trust faster than any sales deck.
  • Evaluate failure modes, not just capabilities. Enterprise buyers care more about "when does it fail?" than "what's your MMLU score?"
🧭 Founder principle: The founder who creates the canonical evaluation for their domain becomes the authority of that domain. This is a strategic asset worth more than the model itself. Publish the eval before the model — it signals intellectual leadership.
⚡ Agentic Lens — Fine-tuning
⚙️ Domain Adaptation Agents

Fine-tuning agents automate the full domain adaptation pipeline: scrape domain corpus, clean and deduplicate, generate Q&A pairs from documents (GPT-4 as synthetic teacher), apply LoRA fine-tuning with hyperparameter search, evaluate on domain benchmark, and iterate until quality threshold is met. What previously required 3-4 ML engineers now runs in a single agentic workflow.

🧬 Synthetic Instruction Generation

Agents generate diverse instruction-following datasets for fine-tuning: given a topic, an agent creates diverse question types (factual, analytical, creative, adversarial), generates high-quality answers, critiques them for accuracy, and filters for quality — producing training data that matches or exceeds expensive human-curated datasets for most domains.

🔁 Iterative Self-Play Fine-tuning

Models fine-tune on their own better outputs: generate responses, filter high-quality ones, fine-tune on them, repeat. Spin, SELF-INSTRUCT, and Evol-Instruct are agentic self-improvement loops. WizardCoder (competitive with GPT-4 on coding) was fine-tuned entirely on self-generated progressively harder problems — no human-written code in training data.

⚡ The domain-specific LLM business model is under pressure precisely because fine-tuning agents make it cheap to create domain-specific models — the competitive moat shifts entirely to proprietary data, not fine-tuning expertise.

Evaluation & Benchmarking

⏱ 1–3 months 👥 2–8 people 💰 $20K–$200K
▼
MMLU (Knowledge)
85%
HumanEval (Code)
72%
GSM8K (Math)
91%
TruthfulQA (Safety)
78%

Before releasing your AI, you need to test it rigorously. We run thousands of standardized tests — math problems, trivia questions, coding tasks — and compare our model's scores against other models. We also test for harmful outputs, biases, and factual errors. Think of it like a final exam before graduation.

Standard benchmarks: MMLU (57-subject knowledge), HellaSwag (commonsense), HumanEval/MBPP (code), GSM8K/MATH (reasoning), TruthfulQA, BIG-Bench Hard, MT-Bench (chat), LMSYS Chatbot Arena (ELO-based human eval). Red-teaming for safety: adversarial prompts, jailbreaks, bias audits, and Constitutional AI evaluations. Eleuther's lm-evaluation-harness is standard.

📜 Evaluation Methodology Timeline
2021BIG-Bench — Srivastava et al. (204 authors) — 204 tasks beyond current capabilities; first collaborative benchmark effort at scale
2021MMLU — Hendrycks et al. — 57 subjects from elementary to professional level; became the standard knowledge benchmark
2022HELM — Liang et al. (Stanford) — holistic evaluation: accuracy + calibration + robustness + fairness + efficiency
2023MT-Bench / Chatbot Arena — Zheng et al. (LMSYS) — GPT-4 as judge; ELO ratings via human A/B comparisons; became community standard
2024GPQA — Rein et al. — PhD-level science questions even experts get 65%; tests genuine knowledge vs pattern matching
2024SWE-Bench — Jimenez et al. — real GitHub issues; tests agent-level code editing capability; harder than HumanEval
🔬 Active Research (2024–25)
  • Benchmark contamination — MMLU, GSM8K likely in pretraining data; inflated scores; decontamination methods active area
  • LLM-as-judge — GPT-4 judge has positional bias, verbosity bias, self-enhancement bias (Zheng et al.)
  • Agent evaluation — SWE-Bench, WebArena, OSWorld test real task completion, not just QA
  • Capability elicitation — can we reliably surface all of a model's capabilities? Chain-of-thought, few-shot changes scores significantly
  • Safety red-teaming — automated red-teaming (Perez et al.), StrongREJECT for jailbreak evaluation
🚀 Open Research Directions
  • Evaluation-proof benchmarks — can we create benchmarks that can't be contaminated? Dynamic, generated-at-eval-time problems
  • Real-world task evaluation — browsing, coding, research assistance; how to standardize?
  • Behavioral consistency — does the model behave the same when deployed vs evaluated?
  • Interpretability as evaluation — mechanistic understanding of capabilities vs black-box measurement

Team Size: 5 – 15 people

💰 Investor Lens — Inference & Deployment
📊 Ongoing OpEx (The Gross Margin Problem)
  • GPU H100 cluster ($1M+/node): $2–$8/hr per node
  • Cost to serve 1M tokens (GPT-4 scale): ~$0.03–$0.12
  • OpenAI charges ~$0.03/1K output tokens → gross margin ~40–60%
  • Quantized/distilled models reduce serving cost by 4–8x
  • Inference is the largest recurring cost line in the P&L
💡 Efficiency = Margin Expansion
  • Flash Attention → 3x throughput → 3x margin improvement
  • Speculative decoding → 2–3x latency reduction
  • INT8/INT4 quantization → 4x cost reduction
  • Batch inference → amortize fixed GPU costs across requests
  • Dedicated hardware (custom ASICs) → 10x long-term cost reduction
📈 Key Investor Metrics
  • Gross Margin %: target >50% at scale (OpenAI: ~40%)
  • Tokens/second/GPU: throughput efficiency
  • P50/P99 latency: time to first token, total latency
  • Cost per 1M tokens: trajectory should decline 50%/yr
  • Uptime SLA: enterprise requires 99.9%+
🚩 Infrastructure Red Flags
  • Gross margin below 30% — unsustainable at scale
  • Single cloud dependency (AWS outage = company outage)
  • No auto-scaling — pays for GPUs 24/7 even at low traffic
  • GPU cost growing faster than revenue
  • No cost monitoring per customer/endpoint
💡 Investor insight: Inference economics determine the long-term business model. A company with 60% gross margins can invest in R&D and win; one with 20% margins is a compute reseller with no future. The best AI companies are obsessed with inference efficiency.
🧭 Founder Lens — Inference & Deployment
💡 Infrastructure as the Moat
  • On-premise deployment is the unaddressed enterprise need. 80% of Fortune 500 companies cannot send sensitive data to OpenAI's cloud due to compliance requirements. The winner of enterprise AI deployment will sell the server rack, not the API.
  • Inference optimization as a service — startups like Anyscale and Fireworks have shown that inference efficiency IS a business model. 3x cheaper inference than OpenAI with the same quality = massive GTM.
  • Edge deployment for regulated industries — air-gapped networks in defense, healthcare, financial services. This market is $50B+ and barely anyone is addressing it with LLMs.
🧭 Founder Operations
  • Set up cost monitoring per customer before you have customers. Knowing your cost per request at the unit level prevents the "growth kills profitability" trap that destroyed many early AI startups.
  • Build latency SLAs into your contracts from day one — this forces engineering discipline and becomes a marketing differentiator.
  • Your inference infrastructure is your production floor. Treat GPU downtime like a factory outage, not a software bug. Build your incident response process before your first enterprise customer.
  • Auto-scaling saves founders from the worst kind of failure: a viral moment that crashes your servers and kills momentum right when you had it.
🧭 Founder principle: The founders who win at deployment think of themselves as infrastructure companies, not AI companies. Infrastructure is boring, sticky, high-margin, and almost impossible to rip out once installed. That's the business you want to be.
⚡ Agentic Lens — Evaluation
🧪 Agentic Eval Frameworks

LLM-as-judge evaluation uses a frontier model to score outputs on quality, faithfulness, helpfulness, and safety — replacing expensive human evaluations for many use cases. Agents run hundreds of test cases in parallel, generate evaluation reports, identify failure patterns, and flag regressions. Braintrust, LangSmith, and Arize Phoenix automate the eval → fix → re-eval loop.

🎭 Adversarial Agent Testing

Specialized adversarial agents play the role of difficult users — asking ambiguous questions, providing contradictory context, testing edge cases, and attempting jailbreaks. These agent "testers" run continuously against production models, providing real-time safety and quality signals without human testers. DeepMind's FunSearch used agent-vs-agent evaluation to discover novel mathematical algorithms.

🌐 Real-world Task Evaluation

Benchmark contamination (models trained on test sets) makes traditional evals unreliable. Agentic evaluation uses tasks that require real tool use — WebArena agents browse real websites, SWE-bench agents fix real GitHub issues, GAIA agents solve multi-step research tasks with web access. These "living evals" cannot be memorized and reflect true capability.

⚡ Agentic evaluation is resolving the benchmark contamination crisis — tasks that require real-world tool use cannot be gamed by memorization, giving researchers the reliable capability signal that static benchmarks lost in 2024.

🏢 Startup Lens — Evaluation (Building Credibility)
💡 Startup Strategy
  • Benchmarks are marketing. A strong MMLU or MT-Bench score is a press release. Mistral's launch was essentially: "We beat LLaMA-2 13B with a 7B model." That one benchmark result closed a $100M round.
  • Submit to LMSYS Chatbot Arena. Free, community-run ELO leaderboard. Appearing above GPT-3.5 is worth more than any marketing campaign for developer credibility.
  • Create a domain benchmark. If you're building a legal AI, create "LegalBench performance" as your primary metric. Own the narrative in your vertical.
  • Red-team before your enterprise pilots. One safety failure in front of a Fortune 500 prospect ends the deal. Budget 2 weeks of adversarial testing before any enterprise conversation.

Now we make it available to users. This means putting the model on powerful servers, compressing it so it runs faster, building an API so apps can talk to it, and scaling up so thousands of people can use it simultaneously. It's like opening a restaurant — you need the kitchen (servers), menu (API), and enough staff (infrastructure) to serve everyone.

Inference optimization: quantization (AWQ, GPTQ, bitsandbytes INT4), speculative decoding, FlashAttention-2, PagedAttention (vLLM), continuous batching, tensor parallelism across GPUs. Serving frameworks: vLLM, TGI, TensorRT-LLM, Triton. For production: rate limiting, safety filters, streaming tokens, observability (latency, TTFT, TPS metrics), and cost per token optimization.

📜 Inference Systems Timeline
2022FlashAttention — Dao et al. (Stanford) — fused CUDA kernel; IO-aware; 2–4× speedup; enabled 10K+ context training
2023Speculative Decoding — Chen et al. (Google) / Leviathan et al. — small draft model proposes tokens; large model verifies in parallel; 2–3× speedup
2023vLLM / PagedAttention — Kwon et al. (UC Berkeley) — virtual memory for KV cache; near-zero KV fragmentation; 24× throughput
2023AWQ — Lin et al. (MIT) — activation-aware weight quantization; INT4 with minimal accuracy loss; hardware-friendly
2024FlashAttention-3 — Shah et al. — asynchronous overlapping of compute and memory on H100; 1.5–2.0× over FA-2
2024SGLang — Zheng et al. — structured generation language; radix attention for KV reuse across requests; 5× throughput
🔬 Active Research (2024–25)
  • Speculative decoding variants — Medusa (multi-head), Eagle (autoregressive draft), SpecInfer; 3–5× practical speedups
  • KV cache compression — StreamingLLM (attention sinks), SnapKV, PyramidKV; compress KV without accuracy loss
  • Edge deployment — MLC-LLM, llama.cpp run 7B on phones; Apple Neural Engine, Qualcomm AI; quantization to 2-4 bits
  • Disaggregated serving — separate prefill and decode across machines (Splitwise, Mooncake)
  • Multi-model serving — heterogeneous clusters; routing queries to right-sized models
🚀 Open Research Directions
  • Hardware-software co-design — Groq, Tenstorrent, Cerebras custom chips; will they displace H100s?
  • Continuous batching at scale — dynamic sequence lengths; optimal scheduling is an open problem
  • Neuromorphic approaches — Intel Loihi, IBM NorthPole; spike-based inference could be 100× more efficient
  • Memory bandwidth wall — LLM inference is memory-bound; DRAM bandwidth limits scale; HBM4, CXL solutions emerging
⏱ Stage Duration: 1 – 4 months (then ongoing)

💰 Investor Lens — Product & Go-to-Market
📊 Revenue Metrics That Matter
  • ARR (Annual Recurring Revenue): target $1M (seed), $10M (Series A), $50M (Series B)
  • NRR (Net Revenue Retention): >120% = world-class (customers expand usage)
  • CAC Payback Period: target <12 months for SMB, <18 months for enterprise
  • Gross Margin: 50–70% for API, 70–85% for SaaS layer on top
  • Magic Number: net new ARR / S&M spend — target >0.75
💡 GTM Moats
  • Developer community → organic distribution (HuggingFace model)
  • Enterprise integration depth → high switching costs
  • API ecosystem → third-party plugins compound the moat
  • Brand trust in regulated industries (healthcare, finance, legal)
  • Usage-based pricing aligns incentives: grow with your customers
📈 Unit Economics Progression
  • Pre-product: Burn only, no revenue
  • Early traction: $10K–$50K MRR, negative unit economics
  • Product-market fit: $100K+ MRR, gross margin positive
  • Scale: $1M+ MRR, clear path to profitability
  • Mature: $10M+ MRR, 60%+ GM, positive EBITDA
🚩 Commercialization Red Flags
  • High gross revenue but poor net revenue retention (<90%)
  • All revenue from one customer (>20% concentration risk)
  • Long sales cycles (>9 months) with no self-serve funnel
  • No product-led growth element — 100% sales-led is expensive
  • Pricing not tied to value — charging per seat not per outcome
💡 Investor insight: Revenue is vanity, NRR is sanity, cash is reality. An AI company with 130%+ NRR is a compounding machine — existing customers grow faster than churn. This single metric predicts long-term success more reliably than ARR growth rate.
🧭 Founder Lens — Product & GTM
💡 Distribution Is the Moat (Not the Model)
  • The model is a commodity; the distribution is the business. OpenAI won not because GPT-4 is infinitely better than competitors, but because they had 100M users generating preference data and network effects before any competitor shipped.
  • Embed inside existing workflows. Cursor won over GitHub Copilot by being inside VSCode. Harvey AI won over generic LLMs by being inside the legal document workflow. Find where your users already live and embed there.
  • Open-source the model, monetize the deployment. HuggingFace, Mistral, Meta with LLaMA — open models create community and distribution. Charge for the managed service, the enterprise features, the compliance layer.
🧭 Finding Your First 10 Customers
  • Your first 10 customers should be people you can call directly. No marketing, no sales team — just founder-led sales to people you know or people who know your work.
  • Charge from day one. Free pilots create no urgency to evaluate. A $5K/month commitment forces real evaluation and real feedback.
  • One design partner who co-creates the product with you is worth 1,000 users who try and churn. Find that design partner before you build anything.
  • Your NPS score from your first 10 customers predicts your long-term NRR better than any projection model.
🚀 2026 GTM Opportunities
  • AI agents that complete multi-step professional workflows end-to-end — not copilots, full autonomous agents
  • Vertical SaaS replacement with AI at the core — replace Salesforce for SMBs with an AI-native CRM
  • AI for non-English markets — localized models + localized GTM in MENA, Southeast Asia, LatAm
  • Compliance-first AI for regulated industries — HIPAA, SOC2, FedRAMP AI products
🧭 Founder principle: The best AI products feel inevitable in hindsight but were non-obvious when built. The pattern: find where knowledge workers spend 30%+ of their time on a repetitive cognitive task, and make AI do that task better than any human can. That's your product.
⚡ Agentic Lens — Deployment
🚀 Self-healing Infrastructure

Deployment agents monitor inference clusters in real-time: detect latency spikes, scale capacity preemptively, restart unhealthy pods, route traffic away from failing nodes, and roll back bad model versions automatically. Mean-time-to-recovery for incidents at OpenAI and Anthropic dropped 60-80% after deploying agentic ops systems versus manual alerting-and-fix workflows.

🔄 Continuous Improvement Loops

Production agents collect user feedback signals (thumbs down, corrections, regeneration requests), identify failure clusters, generate targeted fine-tuning data from failures, trigger automated fine-tuning runs, A/B test the improved model against the baseline, and promote it if metrics improve — a fully automated capability improvement loop with human oversight only at promotion gates.

🛡️ Agentic Safety Monitoring

Safety classifier agents monitor every production response for policy violations, hallucinations, and harmful content — in real-time, at millions of requests per day. These agents flag suspicious patterns, investigate anomalies, generate incident reports, and adapt classifiers as new attack patterns emerge. Traditional keyword filters are replaced by LLM-powered guardrail agents that understand context.

⚡ The LLM deployment stack is becoming an agentic system that manages itself — from infrastructure to safety to quality. The human role in production AI shifts from operations to strategy: setting goals, reviewing reports, and approving major changes.

🏢 Startup Lens — Deployment (Your Revenue Engine)
💡 Startup Strategy
  • API-first launch. Developer APIs (like OpenAI's) scale with zero marginal sales cost. Launch with a simple REST API, generous free tier, and excellent docs. Developers will build your marketing for you.
  • Inference cost is your unit economics. If it costs you $0.002/1K tokens to serve and you charge $0.01/1K tokens, your gross margin is 80%. Model that before launch.
  • Use vLLM on Lambda Labs. 60% cheaper than AWS, production-grade serving. Many Series A AI startups serve millions of requests/day on <$50K/month infra spend.
  • Two-tier pricing from day one. Free/hobbyist tier (builds community + word of mouth) + paid tier (pays the bills). Anthropic's free Claude.ai vs paid API is the template.
  • Enterprise contracts are 10–100× the revenue of API. One Fortune 500 deal at $500K/yr beats 10,000 developer accounts. Build an enterprise tier with SSO, private deployment, SLAs.
💰 Serving Economics
vLLM on Lambda Labs (8× H100)~$14K/month
Same on AWS p4de.24xlarge~$35K/month
Throughput (7B INT4, 8× H100)~5,000 tokens/sec
Revenue at $0.01/1K tokens~$4.3M/month at capacity
💡 Founder tip: Together.ai, Anyscale, and Replicate all started as inference-only companies serving other people's open-source models. You don't need to train to generate revenue — but training gives you a moat.
💰 Investor Lens — Inference & Deployment
Biggest Ongoing OpEx
  • Inference is the largest recurring cost in an AI company's P&L after people
  • H100 node (8× GPUs): $14K–$35K/month depending on cloud provider
  • OpenAI reportedly spends $700K/day on inference at peak load
  • GPU costs eat gross margin — efficiency is survival at scale
  • Industry average gross margin target: 70–85% at scale; <50% = serious concern
Key Metrics Investors Track
  • TTFT (Time to First Token): <500ms for consumer; <200ms for real-time apps
  • Throughput: tokens/second per GPU — measures serving efficiency
  • Cost per token: amortized serving cost vs revenue per token = gross margin
  • Latency P99: tail latency matters for enterprise SLAs
  • GPU utilization: >70% means efficient; <40% means you're burning money on idle capacity
Efficiency = Profit
  • vLLM vs naive serving: 24× throughput improvement = 24× more revenue per GPU
  • Speculative decoding: 2–3× latency reduction with no accuracy loss
  • INT4 quantization: 4× memory reduction = 4× more model instances per GPU
  • Mistral's sliding window attention: 4× faster inference at long context = cost moat
  • Every 10% efficiency improvement at $10M/month GPU spend = $1M/month in EBITDA
Gross Margin Trajectory
  • Gross margin trajectory is the single most important financial metric at Series B+
  • Year 1: 20–40% GM (high GPU cost, low utilization, scale-up costs)
  • Year 2: 50–65% GM (utilization improves, efficiency gains kick in)
  • Year 3+: 70–85% GM (scale benefits, model amortization, efficiency compounding)
  • Investor question: what specific engineering investments will drive GM from X% to Y%?
💡 Investor insight: Inference efficiency is the new hardware advantage. The team that achieves 2× better cost-per-token than competitors can undercut on price AND earn better margins simultaneously — a rare combination that drives both growth rate and unit economics toward the public market benchmark of 70%+ gross margin.
🏢 Startup Playbook

The AI Startup Journey

From idea in a coffee shop to billion-dollar AI company — the real story behind OpenAI, Anthropic, Mistral, and what it takes to repeat it

01

Founding — The Origin Story

How the world's top AI companies got started

🤖
OpenAI (2015)
Sam Altman + Elon Musk + Greg Brockman + Ilya Sutskever + others. Founded as a non-profit with $1B pledged, motivated by fear of Google DeepMind's AI dominance. The key insight: AGI safety required an independent lab not beholden to a tech giant. Converted to "capped-profit" in 2019 to raise VC. Now valued at $157B.
💡 Lesson: A clear mission narrative ("safe AGI for humanity") attracts both top talent and capital who feel part of something historic.
🧬
Anthropic (2021)
Dario Amodei + Daniela Amodei + 7 others left OpenAI after disagreements over safety culture and governance. Raised $124M seed round in weeks — purely on team reputation. Their first product didn't exist. Investors bet on the people. Now at $18B valuation with $7.3B raised.
💡 Lesson: Team credibility is worth more than a product at the seed stage. If you're ex-OpenAI/DeepMind/Google Brain, you can raise before writing a line of code.
🌪️
Mistral AI (2023)
Arthur Mensch (ex-DeepMind) + Guillaume Lample + Timothée Lacroix (both ex-Meta FAIR). Raised €105M seed in June 2023 — largest European seed round ever — with a pitch deck and no product. Released Mistral 7B 4 months later as a torrent file on Twitter. Valued at $6B within 12 months of founding.
💡 Lesson: Open-source as a launch strategy. The torrent tweet generated more press than any ad campaign could. Developer trust was built before the enterprise sales team existed.
📋 Founding Checklist (Do This in Month 1)
Incorporate as Delaware C-Corp (use Stripe Atlas or Clerky — $500, takes 1 day)
83(b) election for all founders within 30 days of incorporation (saves millions in taxes)
4-year vesting schedule with 1-year cliff for all co-founders
IP assignment agreements — all prior work must be assigned to the company
Open a Mercury or Brex startup bank account (free, instant)
Apply for cloud credits: AWS Activate, GCP Startups, Azure, CoreWeave, Lambda Labs
Set up basic legal: YC SAFE template for first check, NDAs, offer letter templates
