🤔 The 5 Questions Every AI Founder Must Answer
1. Why now? What has changed in AI capability, cost, or regulation that makes this possible today but not 2 years ago?
2. Why us? What unfair advantage do you have — unique data access, domain expertise, compute relationships, distribution, or research insight?
3. What is our moat? When GPT-6 launches, why won't it kill your business? (Answer: proprietary data, customer lock-in, domain specialization, or regulation.)
4. Who is our first customer? Not "enterprises" — name the actual company and person who will write the first check. Work backwards from there.
5. What does success look like in 18 months? A specific technical milestone + a specific revenue target + a specific team size. If you can't answer this, you don't have a strategy.
04

Hiring — Building the Team

The order and profiles that matter most at each stage

Founding Team (0→3)
🧠 Technical Co-Founder / CTO
Deep ML expertise. Ideally published researcher. Owns training, architecture, and the technical vision. This person is non-negotiable — don't start without them.
🚀 CEO / Business Co-Founder
Fundraising, vision, sales, hiring. Can be technical (Dario Amodei) or business-focused (Sam Altman). Must be world-class at selling the story.
⚙️ Infra Co-Founder
Systems engineering. Owns training infra, cluster management, and deployment. The difference between a research project and a product company.
Seed Team (3→15)
📋 Head of Data / Data Lead
Hire #4. Data quality determines model quality. This person owns your biggest competitive advantage.
🔬 2–3 Senior ML Researchers
Must have published at NeurIPS/ICML/ICLR. Attract through interesting problems and competitive comp — not just cash. Mission matters enormously to researchers.
🔧 2–3 ML Engineers
Bridge between research and production. Ex-Google Brain, ex-Meta FAIR engineers who can turn a research paper into running code.
💼 Head of GTM / First Sales
Hire early, even at seed. The best technical founders underestimate how long enterprise sales cycles take. Needs 6 months to build pipeline.
Series A Team (15→50)
🛡️ Head of Safety & Alignment
Critical for enterprise trust and regulation compliance. Builds the red-teaming function and policy relationships.
🌐 DevRel & Developer Experience
Your API docs and SDK are your product's front door for developers. One great DevRel engineer is worth 10 salespeople for developer adoption.
📊 VP Engineering
Scales the engineering org. Introduces process without destroying speed. The hardest hire — get this wrong and great engineers leave.
⚖️ Legal + Finance
Outside counsel for IP and contracts. CFO or VP Finance once you have ARR. Don't hire full-time legal until Series B.
🎯 Hiring Tips That Actually Work
📄
Recruit from papers, not resumes. Find the authors of papers you wish you'd written. Email them directly. Response rate is higher than LinkedIn.
🔓
Open-source as recruitment. Mistral released 7B open source partly as a recruiting tool. The best ML engineers wanted to work on the model everyone was downloading.
💰
Pay top of market cash + meaningful equity. Series A startups lose candidates to Google for $100K/yr. Close the gap with equity story and mission — but don't assume mission alone works.
🌍
Remote-first expands your candidate pool 10×. The best ML researcher might be in London, Paris, or Singapore. Most frontier AI companies are now global from day one.
🧪
Paid work trials beat interviews. Offer a 2-week paid trial project before making an offer. You see real work; they experience your culture. Conversion rate to offer is 80%+ if you've done screening right.
⚡
Move fast. Top ML talent gets 3–5 competing offers simultaneously. Compress your process to 2 weeks max. Same-day verbal offers close candidates that would otherwise wait for Google.
05

Infrastructure — Tools & Setup

The exact stack used by modern AI startups, from day one to Series B

Pre-Seed
Google Colab Pro / Vast.ai
$50–$200/month. Good for experiments and prototypes. Not for serious training runs.
Seed
Lambda Labs / CoreWeave
40–60% cheaper than AWS. H100 from $2.49/hr. On-demand or reserved. Best price/performance for AI startups.
Series A
CoreWeave + AWS Hybrid
CoreWeave for training (cost), AWS for serving (reliability). Apply for CoreWeave startup credits ($100K–$500K).
Series B+
Reserved H100 Cluster or Own Hardware
1-year reservations on CoreWeave / Azure / AWS save 30–40%. At 1,000+ GPUs, buying your own DGX nodes has 3-year ROI.
Training
Weights & Biases (W&B)
Free for startups. The standard for experiment tracking, loss curves, hyperparameter sweeps. Every AI startup uses it.
Training Framework
HuggingFace TRL + PEFT
For SFT and RLHF at startup scale. Well-documented, active community, supports LoRA/QLoRA out of the box.
Large-Scale Training
Megatron-LM / PyTorch FSDP
For 70B+ runs. FSDP is built into PyTorch 2.0 and easier to set up than Megatron. Use Megatron only if you need extreme MFU.
Serving
vLLM
Open source, 24× better throughput than naive serving, PagedAttention. The default choice for AI startup inference. Free.
Data Pipeline
HuggingFace Datasets + Datatrove
Standard for loading and preprocessing. Datatrove for large-scale web data pipelines. Both open source.
Model Registry
HuggingFace Hub (private)
$0 for public models, ~$9/month for private. Version control for model weights. Standard in the industry.
Code
GitHub + GitHub Actions
Standard. All training code in private repo. GitHub Actions for CI/CD of eval pipelines and serving deployment.
Docs & Knowledge
Notion
Training logs, architecture decisions, meeting notes, hiring pipelines. $16/user/month. Worth every penny for async teams.
Communication
Slack + Linear
Slack for async comms (training-alerts bot!). Linear for engineering sprints and issue tracking. Both <$10/user/month.
API Backend
FastAPI + Modal
FastAPI for your inference API (Python-native, fast). Modal for serverless GPU functions — great for burst compute without cluster management.
Monitoring
Grafana + Prometheus
Free, self-hosted. Track GPU utilization, request latency, TTFT, error rates. Essential for production serving.
On-Call
PagerDuty (or Opsgenie free)
Rotate on-call during training runs. One missed GPU failure = hours of lost training. <$20/user/month.
Banking
Mercury + Brex
Mercury for main business account (free). Brex for corporate cards with AI startup perks and high limits. Both instant online setup.
Legal
Clerky / Stripe Atlas + Cooley/Wilson Sonsini
Clerky for incorporation ($500 flat). For serious fundraising, engage a startup-specialist law firm (Cooley, Wilson Sonsini, Gunderson) — worth the cost at Series A.
CRM
Attio or HubSpot
Attio is the modern CRM built for startups — free to start. Track investor pipeline AND enterprise customer pipeline in one place.
Payroll & HR
Rippling
Handles payroll, benefits, equity management, device management. Standard for YC companies. $8/employee/month.
Cap Table
Carta
Non-negotiable. Track equity, SAFEs, option pools, and investor rights. $2K–$10K/year. Investors expect you to be on Carta.
Analytics
PostHog (self-hosted)
Open-source product analytics. Track API usage, feature adoption, churn signals. Free self-hosted. $450/month hosted.
06

Go-To-Market — Commercialising Your Model

How to turn a research project into a revenue-generating company

🌱
Phase 1: Developer Launch (Month 1–6)
Goal: 1,000 active API users, 10 design partners
Launch on HuggingFace Release model weights publicly (or gated). HuggingFace gets 5M monthly visitors. Mistral's 7B release got 50K downloads in week one.
Twitter/X launch thread The AI community is on Twitter. A compelling benchmark thread from a credible account gets 10K+ retweets. Mistral launched with a torrent link in a tweet.
Private beta waitlist Framer, Notion, and Figma all built pre-launch hype with waitlists. Collect 500 emails before you have an API. Use Typeform + Airtable.
Design partners Find 5–10 companies who will use your model in production in exchange for early access + their feedback shapes your roadmap. These become your first case studies.
📈
Phase 2: Developer-Led Growth (Month 6–18)
Goal: $500K ARR, 50 paying enterprise pilots
Best-in-class docs & SDK OpenAI's documentation is a competitive moat. Developers who learn your API become advocates. Invest 1 engineer full-time on developer experience.
Benchmark leadership Own a leaderboard position. "Fastest inference at 7B scale" or "Best coding model under $0.01/1K tokens" is a marketing hook that writes itself.
Community flywheel Discord server + open-source ecosystem + hackathons. Perplexity ran hackathons that produced 200+ demos, each one a marketing asset.
Outbound enterprise Use design partners as case studies. One VP Eng at a mid-market company is worth 500 developer signups in revenue. Start outbound at Month 6 even if product feels unready.
🏢
Phase 3: Enterprise Scale (Month 18+)
Goal: $10M ARR, 3+ named enterprise customers
Enterprise sales motion Hire a VP Sales with enterprise SaaS experience (not just AI experience). Add: SOC2 Type II certification, BAA for healthcare, enterprise SLAs.
Partner ecosystem System integrator partnerships (Accenture, Deloitte) can 10× your enterprise pipeline. They implement AI for Fortune 500s and need models to recommend.
Government / regulated sector US Federal, EU public sector, healthcare, finance — all have budget and high WTP for compliant AI. Longer sales cycles but $1M+ contracts.
07

Revenue — Business Models & Path to Profit

How AI companies actually make money

⚡
API / Token Pricing
OpenAI: $0.002–$0.06/1K tokens | Anthropic: $0.003–$0.015/1K
Pay-per-use. Scales automatically. Low friction to start. 70–85% gross margins at scale. Best for developer-first companies.
Start here. Launch on day one.
🏢
Enterprise Contracts
Typical: $200K–$5M/year. Harvey AI: $100M+ ARR from law firms.
Annual contracts with SLAs, private deployment, custom fine-tuning, priority support. High ACV, long sales cycle (3–12 months), but very sticky.
Build enterprise tier at Month 6–12.
👤
Consumer Subscription
ChatGPT Plus: $20/month → 10M subscribers = $2.4B/year ARR
B2C SaaS. High volume, lower ACV. Requires strong product + marketing. CAC must be <6 months of LTV. Very hard to make work without a dominant product position.
Add only if you have strong B2C traction. Don't split focus early.
🔧
Fine-Tuning as a Service
OpenAI charges $0.008/1K tokens for fine-tuning. Together.ai offers full pipeline.
Customers bring their own data; you train a custom model version. High margin, creates deep lock-in. Differentiates from pure API players.
Add at Series A once you have serving infra.
📦
On-Premise / Private Cloud
Cohere offers on-prem. Typical: $1M–$10M/year for large enterprises.
Deploy model inside customer's infrastructure. Required for regulated industries (banking, defense, healthcare). Highest ACV but operationally complex.
Add at Series B when you have ops capacity.
📊 Unit Economics That Investors Want to See
Gross Margin
70–85%
API businesses at scale. <50% = serving too expensive; revisit quantization.
Net Revenue Retention
>120%
Customers should expand usage over time. OpenAI's NRR is estimated >150%.
CAC Payback
<12 months
How long to recover customer acquisition cost. Enterprise <18 months is acceptable.
Magic Number
>0.75
New ARR / Sales & Marketing spend. Above 0.75 = efficient growth; above 1.5 = accelerate spend.
08

Founder Tips — Hard-Won Lessons

What the founders of OpenAI, Anthropic, Mistral, Cohere, and others wish they'd known

⚠️
Avoid the "Research Trap"
The most common failure mode: brilliant researchers who build impressive models but no business. Set a revenue target from day one — even $10K ARR in month 6 forces you to talk to customers. Many AI companies have died with state-of-the-art benchmarks and zero customers.
🎯
Don't Compete on Scale
You cannot out-compute Google or Microsoft. Your edge must be: better training data in a vertical, a unique deployment approach, a proprietary feedback loop from users, or a distribution advantage. Win the niche first, then expand.
🤝
Co-Founder Chemistry is Everything
AI startups are 2–5 year marathons with constant crises. Pick co-founders you've worked with, not just admired. The stress of a failed training run at 2 AM will reveal character. Anthropic's leadership team had worked together at OpenAI for years before founding.
💸
Runway is Sacred
Keep 18 months of runway at all times. AI companies burn fast — a 1,000 GPU training run can cost $5M in 3 months. Raise before you need it. The moment you're desperate for money, your negotiating leverage disappears and your team senses the stress.
📣
Publish or Perish (Recruiting)
The best ML researchers want to work on interesting problems AND publish. Allowing publication (even of non-core IP) attracts top talent that would otherwise go to academia or FAANG. Mistral, Cohere, and AI2 all publish actively. OpenAI publishing GPT-1/2/3 papers built their talent brand.
🔄
Your First Product Will Be Wrong
OpenAI's first product was a gaming AI (Dota 2). Anthropic initially focused on interpretability research before pivoting to Claude. Mistral released models before having a clear application strategy. Stay close to customers, iterate fast, don't fall in love with your first hypothesis.
🌍
Regulation is Coming — Get Ahead
EU AI Act is law. US EO on AI is active. Enterprise customers will ask for safety audits, data governance, and compliance documentation. Startups that build safety and compliance infrastructure early will have a competitive advantage as regulation tightens. Safety is a moat.
🚀
Speed Wins in AI
The AI landscape changes faster than any sector in history. Mistral went from founding to $6B valuation in 12 months. Cursor went from 0 to $9B in 2 years. The window for any given opportunity is shorter than in traditional software. Bias heavily toward action over deliberation.

05
The Hard Realities of Raising Money
What no one tells you before you start — the brutal honest math of fundraising
📉
Top VCs fund <1% of deals they see. Sequoia sees 3,000+ companies per year and funds ~15–20. That's a 0.5% acceptance rate. Getting to a first meeting is itself an achievement.
⏰
Average time to close a round: 6–9 months. Fundraising is a full-time job. During a raise, CEOs spend 60–80% of their time on investor meetings instead of building the company — a real opportunity cost.
📊
Dilution is cumulative and brutal. If you raise 5 rounds and give up 20% each time, you own 32% of the company you started. After a typical VC-backed path to IPO, founders often own 5–15%.
⬇️
Down rounds destroy morale and cap tables. Stability AI raised at a $1B valuation in 2022, then faced reported financial difficulties in 2024. A down round (raising at lower valuation) creates preference stack problems and demoralizes employees.
🌉
Bridge rounds are a warning signal, not a solution. A bridge round (short-term debt/equity to extend runway) buys time but doesn't fix the underlying problem. Investors in bridge rounds often demand punitive terms (2x liquidation preference).
🔒
Board seats mean losing control decisions. After a Series B, founders typically control 2 of 5 board seats. Major decisions (selling the company, firing the CEO, approving budgets over $X) require board approval. Investor-friendly terms accumulate.
💀
90% of AI startups fail — often not from bad technology. Most fail from running out of money, not from a bad model. The #1 cause of startup death: too slow to find product-market fit before the runway ends. Technical excellence without business sense is fatal.
🤐
"No" often means "not yet." 73% of investors who passed on Airbnb's seed round reportedly wish they hadn't. Most VCs that passed on OpenAI's Series A are deeply regretful. Keep relationship-building even with investors who decline.
06
Hacks & Tips for Raising Capital
Tactics that actually work — from founders who've raised $10M to $10B
🤝
Warm Intros Convert 7x Better
Cold emails to VCs have <5% response rates. Warm intros from portfolio founders convert 7x better. Build your investor network before you need it — attend conferences, publish technical work, be generous with advice to other founders.
📊
Lead With Traction, Not Vision
Revenue beats slides every time. Even $10K MRR is compelling at seed stage. Three enterprise pilots with signed LOIs beat 50 slides of market analysis. Show real evidence of demand, not theoretical TAM.
⚡
Create Competitive FOMO
Run a tight process: start conversations with 30+ investors simultaneously, set a hard deadline for term sheets ("we're closing in 3 weeks"), share that you have competitive interest. FOMO closes rounds faster than any pitch deck.
🔢
Know Your Numbers Cold
Investors ask: "What's your burn rate?" "What's your 18-month runway?" "What are your unit economics?" "What does $10M of Series A get us?" If you hesitate, you lose. Rehearse financial answers until instant.
📖
The Pitch Narrative Arc
Best pitches follow: (1) The world is changing → (2) We have a unique insight → (3) Our solution captures it → (4) Here's proof it works → (5) This is the team to do it → (6) We need $X to reach $Y milestone. Never lead with the product.
📁
Data Room Checklist
Have ready before any meeting: cap table (with all instruments), last 12 months P&L, model card / technical overview, customer contracts + NDA, reference customer list, team bios + LinkedIn, IP assignment agreements, incorporation docs.
🎯
Target Right-Fit Investors
A no from Sequoia means nothing if they don't invest at your stage. Research: What stage do they lead? What check sizes? Do they have competing portfolio companies? Have they invested in AI before? 20 right-fit investors > 200 wrong ones.
⚖️
Negotiate Terms, Not Just Valuation
Valuation matters less than: pro-rata rights (can you invest in future rounds?), board composition, liquidation preference (1x non-participating is founder-friendly; 2x participating is not), and anti-dilution provisions. Get a startup lawyer on day one.

The Rules of Financial Discipline
🔴
18-Month Runway Rule
Always raise your next round when you have 18 months of runway remaining. Not 6 months (desperation pricing). Not 24 months (leaving dilution money on the table). 18 months is the Goldilocks zone.
📊
Monthly Financial Cadence
Send investor updates every month: actual vs. budget P&L, cash runway, key metrics (ARR, MRR, burn), top 3 wins, top 3 risks, and specific asks. Investors who feel informed write bigger follow-on cheques.
💼
When to Hire a CFO
Hire a fractional CFO at Series A ($10M+ raised). Hire a full-time VP Finance at Series B ($30M+ raised). Before that, use accounting software (QuickBooks, Pilot.com) plus a good startup accountant. Don't let financial oversight slip.
⚠️
Burn Discipline is Survival
Most AI startups die from running out of money before they find product-market fit — not from bad technology. A company that extends runway by 6 months through cost cuts has that much more time to find the insight that changes everything.

Path to IPO & Exit Strategies
When and how the biggest AI companies go public — and what the alternatives look like
🏛️ IPO
When: $100M+ ARR, >50% gross margin, path to profitability
Pros: Maximum valuation, liquidity for all shareholders, M&A currency, brand prestige, talent attraction
Cons: 6–12 month process, $10M+ in legal/banking fees, public scrutiny of finances, quarterly earnings pressure, lock-up period (6 months where insiders can't sell)
Examples: No pure AI LLM companies have IPO'd yet (as of 2025). CoreWeave IPO'd in 2025 as AI infra play.
🤝 Strategic Acquisition
When: Strong technology + team, acquirer needs AI capability fast
Pros: Certainty of outcome, fast close (3–6 months), immediate liquidity, distribution from acquirer
Cons: Often below peak valuation, culture clash risk, earn-out provisions, losing independence
Inflection AI → Microsoft ($650M talent acquisition), Adept → Amazon, Character.ai → Google ($2.7B acqui-hire)
📈 Secondary Sales
When: Employees and early investors need liquidity before IPO
Pros: Employees can monetize equity without IPO; no dilution if buying from existing shareholders
Cons: Complex to arrange; requires company permission; pricing is opaque; not available to all employees
Platforms: Forge Global, Carta, Hiive. OpenAI employees sold shares at $86B+ valuation pre-IPO.

Founder Lessons on Money & Investment
What the people who built the world's most valuable AI companies learned the hard way
Sam Altman
CEO, OpenAI — raised $13B from Microsoft, $6.6B in 2024
"Compute is the oil of the AI era. Whoever controls the most compute at the best cost will win. We secured our compute supply chain before worrying about revenue. Most startups get this backwards."
💡 Secure your compute supply chain early — it's your production capacity.
Dario Amodei
CEO, Anthropic — raised $7.3B+ from Google, Amazon, Spark Capital
"Safety isn't a cost center — it's what lets us raise at 30x revenue and command premium enterprise pricing. Constitutional AI isn't just ethics, it's our business model."
💡 Safety and alignment are a business moat, not just a moral obligation.
Arthur Mensch
CEO, Mistral AI — raised €1.05B at €6B valuation in 18 months
"We trained a model comparable to GPT-4 for a fraction of the cost by being obsessively efficient. Efficiency is a business model. Investors funded our second model before the first launched — credibility from technical output, not sales."
💡 Technical efficiency is a fundraising story. Publish your results and let the work speak.
Emad Mostaque
Founder, Stability AI — raised $101M, stepped down amid financial pressure 2024
"We moved incredibly fast and created extraordinary technology — but growth without financial discipline catches up with you. Revenue has to follow model capability. You can't indefinitely raise on potential."
⚠️ Cautionary tale: even groundbreaking technology fails without business fundamentals.
Clement Delangue
CEO, Hugging Face — raised $395M at $4.5B valuation
"Our entire GTM is community. We gave away the platform for free, built the open-source AI ecosystem, and enterprises came to us with their wallets open. Community is distribution that no amount of sales spend can replicate."
💡 Open-source community is a $0-CAC distribution channel worth hundreds of millions.
Reid Hoffman
Co-founder LinkedIn / Partner Greylock — invested in OpenAI, Inflection, others
"In AI, the capital requirements have compressed the normal VC timeline. Your Series A is someone else's seed round. Founders need to think bigger and move faster than any previous era of software. And calibrate: in AI, 'fast' means 6-month model cycles, not 2-year product cycles."
💡 AI timelines are compressed. What took 4 years in SaaS takes 18 months in AI.
🧭 Founder's Compass

The Founder's Perspective

Finding gaps, building conviction, attracting talent, managing yourself and others — everything the great AI founders learned that isn't in any textbook

01
Finding the Gap — Ideas Nobody Is Talking About
The most valuable opportunities in 2025–26 AI are hiding in plain sight
🔥 Hot but Undercrowded
Domain-Specific Reasoning Models
Legal reasoning, medical diagnosis, financial analysis — models that don't just generate text but reason through multi-step professional decisions with verifiable logic chains. No frontier lab is prioritizing this.
Why now: o3/o1-style reasoning + domain data = 10x better than GPT-4 on professional tasks
🔥 Hot but Undercrowded
Agentic Workflow Automation
Not copilots — fully autonomous agents that complete 10-step professional workflows end-to-end without human confirmation. The RPA market ($13B) is ready to be rebuilt on LLMs.
Why now: tool-use APIs + long context + reliability thresholds crossed in 2024–25
❄️ Cold but Massive
Non-English Frontier Models
3.5 billion people speak no English. Arabic, Hindi, Swahili, Tagalog, and 40+ other languages have essentially zero high-quality frontier models. This is the biggest untapped market in AI.
Market size: the next billion AI users will not speak English
❄️ Cold but Massive
AI for Physical World Data
Sensor data, industrial IoT, satellite imagery, seismic data, agricultural telemetry — none of these are in LLM training sets. Foundation models for physical-world data are 3–5 years behind text LLMs.
Who wins: the company that trains the "GPT-4 of sensor data"
👁️ Hidden Gems
On-Premise Enterprise AI
80% of Fortune 500 data never leaves their firewall for compliance reasons. The on-premise LLM market is $20B+ and almost no startup is seriously pursuing it. Sell the box, not the API.
One $5M enterprise on-premise contract = 10x better economics than 50 API customers
👁️ Hidden Gems
AI-Native Vertical SaaS
Replacing entire legacy SaaS products (not adding AI to them) with AI-native alternatives. An AI-native EHR that eliminates 90% of documentation burden is a $100B opportunity. Harvey AI is doing this for legal.
The incumbents are too slow to self-cannibalize. The window is 2024–2027.
How to Find Your Gap — The 3-Filter Framework
1
Pain Filter
Find a specific person (not a market) who spends 30%+ of their working day on a cognitive task that feels repetitive, frustrating, and beneath their expertise. That task is your product.
2
Timing Filter
Could this have been built 3 years ago? If yes, ask why it wasn't and whether that barrier still exists. The best opportunities couldn't have been built until very recently — but can be built now.
3
Defensibility Filter
If OpenAI dedicated 10 engineers to this for 6 months, could they replicate your advantage? If yes, it's not a startup idea — it's a feature. Find the thing they can't or won't build.
02
Is 2026 the Right Time to Start a Frontier Model Company?
An honest answer — and the real opportunities if frontier isn't your path
❌ Probably Not for Frontier Models
Capital requirements have exploded. In 2020, $10M could train a competitive model. In 2026, frontier training runs cost $50M–$500M+. The barrier has grown 50x in 5 years.
The incumbents have entrenched moats. OpenAI has 300M+ users generating preference data daily. Anthropic has $7B+ in compute contracts. Google has TPU infrastructure that took 10 years to build. These are not replicable.
Talent consolidation. 70% of frontier ML researchers work at 5 companies. Recruiting 10 frontier researchers for a new lab in 2026 requires a compelling story and $50M+ in compensation packages.
✅ Yes — If You Focus on These
🏥 Vertical AI
Healthcare, legal, finance, construction — specialized models that outperform GPT-4 in one domain. This doesn't require frontier compute.
🔧 AI Infrastructure
Inference optimization, fine-tuning platforms, evals-as-a-service, observability for AI — the "picks and shovels" of the AI gold rush. Every AI company is a potential customer.
🤖 AI Agents
Autonomous agents for specific professional workflows. The agent stack (planning, memory, tool use, verification) is almost entirely unbuilt. This is where GPT-2 was in 2019.
🌍 Non-English AI
Build the best LLM for Arabic, Hindi, Portuguese, or Swahili. The TAM is 2–3 billion potential users. The competition is near-zero. This is a 2019-equivalent opportunity.
🏭 AI for Physical World
Robotics, manufacturing, agriculture, energy — domains where AI is 10 years behind language models. Embodied AI, process control, predictive maintenance.
🛡️ AI Safety & Governance
Evals, red-teaming, interpretability tools, compliance platforms, AI audit software. Every AI deployment creates demand for this. Regulatory tailwinds incoming.
03
Building Your Strategy Around the Idea
From insight to company — the strategic decisions that determine everything
1
Start With One Customer, Not One Market
Name a specific person at a specific company who will pay you $5,000/month on day one. If you can't name them, your strategy is too abstract. The customer who exists beats the market that might exist.
2
Define Your "Why Us, Why Now, Why This"
Write a single paragraph that explains why your team is uniquely suited to solve this problem, why this specific moment makes it possible, and why this specific approach is better than alternatives. If you can't write it clearly, you haven't figured out your strategy yet.
3
Choose Your Sequencing
Land and expand beats boil the ocean. Win one hospital system before going after all of healthcare. Win one law firm before going after all of legal. Depth of penetration in one segment creates the proof points needed to expand.
4
Build Your Unfair Advantage Stack
Layer three defensible assets: (1) proprietary data that competitors can't easily get, (2) technical differentiation built on that data, (3) customer relationships and switching costs built on that technology. Each layer amplifies the others.
5
Set Your 18-Month Milestones
Fundraising, hiring, product, and revenue milestones for the next 18 months — specific enough that you'll know in real-time if you're on track. The company that hits milestones on time builds investor trust; the one that misses them dies quietly.
04
Attracting Talent — Getting Great People to Believe in You
The hardest part of building an AI company in 2026 is not the model — it's the team
🧲
Mission > Money (for the first 10)
Your first 10 hires won't join for the salary — they'll join because they believe in what you're building and want to be part of something important. If you can't articulate why this matters beyond revenue, you can't recruit A-players early.
📄
Publish Technical Work First
The fastest way to recruit top researchers is to publish work they respect before you recruit. A paper on arXiv with 500 citations is better than a recruiter with a $50K placement fee. Show the work; the talent follows.
🏆
Hire for Trajectory, Not Resume
The best early hires are people on a steep upward curve — 2nd author at a top lab, not 15th author at OpenAI. Find the researchers who are about to break out and give them the opportunity to lead rather than follow.
💰
Equity as Partnership, Not Compensation
Frame equity as co-ownership, not a lottery ticket. Show them the dilution math, the cap table, the realistic outcomes. Founders who are transparent about equity mechanics build more trust than those who hand out vague promises.
🌐
Build in Public to Attract in Private
Tweet about your technical progress. Post on LinkedIn about what you're building and why. Give talks at conferences before you have a product. The best candidates are passive — they need to discover you, not respond to a cold InMail.
🤝
The Referral Network Is Everything
In AI, the best engineers know each other. Your 3rd hire refers your 4th, who refers your 5th. Treat every early hire as a recruiting node. Ask every candidate: "Who's the best engineer you've worked with who might be available?"
05
Founder Rules, Behaviours & Mental Models
The operating principles that separate founders who build lasting companies from those who don't
⚡
Speed is a Strategy
In AI, being 6 months faster than a competitor is not just an advantage — it's existential. Every decision that can be made today should be made today. Perfect is the enemy of shipped.
🎯
Say No to Almost Everything
Every partnership, conference, advisory board, and feature request is a no by default. Your most scarce resource is focus. The best founders say no to 95% of opportunities so they can say yes fully to the 5% that matters.
📣
Communicate Obsessively
Overcommunicate context, strategy, and priorities to your team. The #1 cause of founder-team misalignment is information asymmetry. Every team member should know the 3 most important things happening this week.
🧪
Be Hypothesis-Driven
Treat every major decision as an experiment with a clear hypothesis, test, and success metric. "We believe X is true. We'll know in 30 days because we'll measure Y." This turns uncertainty into data.
👂
Listen More Than You Talk
In customer meetings, aim for 70% listening and 30% talking. In investor meetings, flip it. In team meetings, calibrate to what the conversation needs. The founder who listens well is rare — and much more effective.
💪
Protect Your Energy
A startup is a marathon disguised as a sprint. Sleep 7–8 hours. Exercise 4x/week. Take one full day off per week. The CEO who burns out in year one is replaced; the one who builds sustainable capacity runs the company for 10 years.
🪞
Radical Self-Awareness
Know your blind spots. Get a coach. Ask your team for honest feedback quarterly. The founder who thinks they have no weaknesses is the most dangerous person in the company.
🔄
Embrace Being Wrong
You will be wrong about your market, your product, and your team multiple times. The skill isn't being right — it's updating fast when you're wrong. Founders who can't change their minds die slowly with their original assumptions.
06
Public Persona, Positioning & Taking Authority
In the AI era, the founder's brand IS the company's brand — especially at the start
🎤
Become the Voice of Your Domain
Pick one problem in your space and talk about it constantly, publicly, and with more depth than anyone else. Not your company — the problem. When people think of that problem, they think of you. Then you announce the solution: your product.
Examples: Andrew Ng on AI education, Andrej Karpathy on LLM internals, Sam Altman on AI safety and acceleration — each owns a narrative position that predates and outlasts any single product.
✍️
Write to Build Authority
One deeply researched long-form essay per month. Post on LinkedIn, Substack, and arXiv where relevant. Writing that teaches something new creates compounding credibility — a blog post from 2021 still generates inbound in 2026.
🐦
Social Media as Recruiting & Sales
X/Twitter in AI is uniquely high-signal. The best ML researchers, investors, and enterprise buyers read it daily. Post technical insights, share honest opinions, and engage in technical debates. Follower count is a lagging indicator — quality of your content is leading.
🏛️
Position the Company, Then the Product
Category design beats product marketing. Don't position your product against competitors — position your company as the creator of a new category. "We're not a better chatbot; we're the first AI that actually understands clinical workflows." Own the category before you own the market.
🤝
Strategic Public Relationships
Be visible at 3 conferences per year — not more. Prioritize quality of relationship over quantity of appearances. One deep conversation with a future design partner at NeurIPS is worth 20 panel appearances at generic tech conferences.
🎯
Own a Contrarian Point of View
Safe, mainstream opinions are forgettable. The founders who build audiences have specific, well-reasoned, contrarian views on the future. "I believe LLMs will replace 40% of knowledge worker tasks by 2028 — here's why, with specifics." Conviction is magnetic.
07
When to Start, When to Pivot, When to Stop
The decisions that require the most courage — and the clearest frameworks
🟢 When to Start
  • You've found a problem you'd work on for 10 years regardless of outcome
  • You've talked to 20+ potential customers who say "I would pay for this today"
  • You have (or can hire) the specific domain + technical combination needed — and no one else does
  • The technology required now exists and didn't 18 months ago
  • You have 18+ months of personal financial runway or are prepared to raise immediately
  • You've tried to talk yourself out of it for 6 months and can't stop thinking about it
🟡 When to Pivot
  • You've been selling for 6 months and fewer than 3 people have paid you anything
  • Your NPS score from existing users is below 30 consistently
  • A competitor shipped your product better 3 months after you started
  • Your team is working hard but nobody is excited about the product anymore
  • You're building features but not solving the core pain point that prompted you to start
  • You have adjacent data/technology that solves a problem 10x better than your current product
🔴 When to Stop
  • You have less than 3 months of runway and no realistic path to raise or reach profitability
  • Your co-founders have irreconcilable disagreements about strategy or values
  • You've pivoted 3+ times and still have no paying customers after 2 years
  • The market shifted and your core assumption is now provably wrong (not "hard" — wrong)
  • A strategic acquirer offers to give your team and technology a better home
  • You've lost conviction in the mission and are just going through the motions
🧭 Founder principle: The decision to stop is often the hardest and most underrated founder skill. The best founders know the difference between a bad week and a broken company. Pivoting too early kills companies; stopping too late kills careers. Use the framework, trust your gut, and talk to mentors who have no stake in your continuation.
08
Daily Knowledge Habits — Staying Ahead of a Fast Market
AI moves at a pace where being 3 months behind feels like 3 years. Here's how the best founders stay current
Daily (30 min)
Morning Intelligence Routine
arXiv cs.AI/cs.CL — scan abstracts of new papers before 9am; read 1–2 full papers per week
X/Twitter AI community — follow @karpathy, @sama, @ylecun, @goodfellow, @fchollet, @emollick, @GaryMarcus for diverse signal
The Rundown AI and Import AI newsletters — curated daily summaries, no noise
Hugging Face Papers — most important papers highlighted daily by the community
Weekly (2–3 hrs)
Deep Learning Ritual
Latent Space Podcast — technical interviews with frontier researchers and practitioners
Lex Fridman Podcast — long-form founder/researcher conversations
TWIML AI Podcast — machine learning research breakdowns
Ben Evans Newsletter — macro AI strategy and business model analysis
One benchmark review — look at the LMSYS Chatbot Arena leaderboard weekly to track model improvements
Monthly
Strategic Recalibration
Read one book by or about a founder/CEO you admire. Not AI books — leadership, psychology, history. Build a multi-domain mental model.
AI Safety research digest — Anthropic, DeepMind, and ARC Evals publish monthly. Regulatory changes here affect your business model.
Competitor analysis sprint — 2 hours reviewing competitor products, pricing, and messaging changes. What changed? Why?
Customer success review — listen to 5 customer calls. The market tells you its needs; most founders stop listening after product-market fit.
Making Yourself Available — Without Losing Your Sanity
📧
Email: Respond to first-time inbound from researchers, potential customers, and thoughtful community members within 24 hours. Nothing builds reputation faster than being responsive when you don't have to be.
🗓️
Office Hours: 2 hours per week publicly available — open calendar link for 30-min slots. This surfaces talent, customer pain, and partnership opportunities you'd never find otherwise.
🛑
Protect Focus Blocks: Block 9am–1pm daily as no-meeting deep work. The founder who is always in meetings stops being a founder and becomes a coordinator. Guard your thinking time ferociously.
🤝
Peer founder network: Build a group of 5–8 non-competing founders at similar stages. Meet monthly. This is your board of directors for personal decisions — honest advice from people with skin in the game.
09
Delegation, Managing People & Stakeholders
The transition from builder to leader is the hardest thing most technical founders face
🔄
The Delegation Ladder
Level 1 "Here's exactly what to do and how to do it" — use for week one of any role
Level 2 "Here's the outcome I need; you decide how" — use after 30 days of demonstrated competence
Level 3 "Here's the area you own; update me weekly on your top priorities" — use with senior hires after 90 days
Level 4 "Here's the mission; you have full autonomy; I'll support when you need it" — use with your best people on their best work
💼
Managing Investors
Send monthly updates — always. Include: metrics (good and bad), highlights, lowlights, and specific asks. Investors who feel informed become advocates; investors who feel surprised become adversaries. Never hide bad news — they'll find out, and the trust damage is permanent.
📊
Managing the Board
Run board meetings like a CEO, not a student presenting to professors. You set the agenda. You decide what decisions need board input. You come with recommendations, not open questions. Board members respect founders who lead their boards — and worry about those who don't.
👥
Managing Your Team Through Growth
1–10 people: Know every person deeply; weekly 1:1s; flat hierarchy; founder directly involved in all key decisions
10–50 people: Build management layer; monthly company all-hands; OKRs or similar goal framework; formal performance reviews
50–200 people: VP layer required; culture deliberate not emergent; promotion criteria written; values documented and enforced
200+ people: You are now primarily a culture and strategy leader. Hire a COO. Your job is clarity of mission, not operational excellence.
💸
Managing Shareholders
Cap table hygiene from day one: use Carta, standardize SAFE/equity terms, keep the cap table clean. A messy cap table with undocumented side deals kills M&A and IPO processes. Every angel investor who feels ignored becomes a potential complication in a future deal.
⚡
Firing Quickly, Hiring Slowly
The worst management mistake founders make is keeping underperformers too long out of loyalty or discomfort. A high performer's respect for the organization evaporates when they see underperformance tolerated. Fire fast, fire kind, and do it yourself — never delegate the first termination.
10
Managing Success, Failure & Your Own Psychology
The inner game of founding — what nobody prepares you for
⚠️
Success Is the Harder Test
Most founders are prepared for failure. Few are prepared for rapid success. Hypergrowth creates: hiring mistakes (speed over fit), culture dilution (can't onboard 10 people/month without culture decay), founder ego (early success is often luck misattributed to genius), and the trap of optimizing for looking successful rather than being successful.
🔁
The Failure Recovery Protocol
1. Give yourself 24–48 hours to feel it fully. Don't suppress.
2. Write a specific post-mortem: what happened, why, what was within your control, what wasn't.
3. Share it with your board and team. Transparency builds trust in adversity.
4. Identify the single most important change to prevent recurrence.
5. Move. The best founders process fast, decide fast, and don't ruminate.
🪤
The Imposter Syndrome Trap
Almost every founder feels like a fraud at some point — usually right before a breakthrough. The founder interviewing for a $50M investment feels less capable than the executive they're pitching. This is normal. The antidote isn't confidence — it's evidence. Keep a "wins file" of real evidence that your approach is working. Read it on bad days.
🧘
Sustainable Founder Psychology
Sam Altman, Dario Amodei, and Jensen Huang all talk about the importance of equanimity — the ability to feel the lows without letting them define the trajectory. Meditation, journaling, therapy, and a trusted personal board (not business advisors) are operational tools, not optional luxuries. The startup is a 10-year project. Plan your psychology accordingly.
📊
Separate Identity from Outcome
Your company failing is not you failing. Your product not shipping on time is not your worth as a person. The founders who survive the emotional rollercoaster have separated their self-worth from their company's metrics. Practice this deliberately. Your value to the world is not your ARR.
🌱
The Long Game
OpenAI was founded in 2015 and ChatGPT launched in 2022 — 7 years. Anthropic raised its first round in 2021 and became a household name in 2023 — 2 years. The timelines in AI can be compressed by breakthrough moments you can't predict. The founder who is still building in year 5 has an enormous advantage over the one who burned out in year 2.
11
Lessons from the Greatest Founders & CEOs in AI
What they actually learned — beyond the official narrative
Jensen Huang
CEO, NVIDIA — turned a gaming GPU company into the backbone of the AI revolution ($3T market cap)
"I always knew the destination. I didn't always know the path. The company I kept describing — a company that would be essential to the future of computing — I kept that vision constant even when the product pivoted completely from gaming to data centers to AI. The strategy changed. The destination didn't."
🔑 Constant destination, flexible path. Revisit your product strategy quarterly; revisit your mission never.
Sam Altman
CEO, OpenAI — went from YC president to leading the most important technology company of the decade
"The thing that separates the best founders is their ability to recruit. It's the highest-leverage thing you can do. I've seen $10M rounds and $100M rounds — the biggest predictor of success is whether the founder can convince extraordinary people to bet their careers on them."
🔑 Recruiting is your most important job until you have 50 people. Then it's still your most important job.
Dario Amodei
CEO, Anthropic — left OpenAI to build an AI safety-first frontier lab
"We made a bet: if powerful AI is coming regardless, it's better to have safety-focused labs at the frontier than to cede that ground to labs less focused on safety. This is a deeply uncomfortable position — we're building the thing we're also trying to make safe. But we think it's better than the alternative."
🔑 Mission-driven companies attract mission-driven talent and investors. Articulate your why clearly and live it visibly.
Arthur Mensch
CEO, Mistral AI — raised €1.05B in 18 months by publishing world-class models with minimal resources
"We published Mistral 7B before we had funding for the next model. We published the weights openly. We had no product yet. But that one release told every investor everything they needed to know about our team's capabilities. Let the work speak first."
🔑 Technical credibility is your most powerful fundraising asset. Create it in public before you need it in private.
Andrej Karpathy
Ex-Tesla AI Director, Ex-OpenAI — the most influential AI educator and practitioner of his generation
"The best way to understand AI systems is to build them from scratch, even tiny versions. You can't really reason about something you haven't built. The CEO who has trained a small neural network makes better decisions than the one who has only read about them."
🔑 Stay technical enough to know when you're being bullshitted. Founders who lose this instinct become dependent on intermediaries.
Fei-Fei Li
Co-director, Stanford HAI; Co-founder, World Labs — the scientist who catalyzed modern AI with ImageNet
"ImageNet took us 3 years and $1M to build, and no one thought it would matter. The most important contributions often look unimportant from the inside. Build infrastructure for the field, not just for your product. Infrastructure builders become indispensable."
🔑 Building shared infrastructure (datasets, benchmarks, tools) creates goodwill, citations, and authority that money can't buy.
Emad Mostaque
Founder, Stability AI — cautionary tale and genuine pioneer
"We moved faster than anyone. We democratized AI art, image generation, and open-source AI models. But we didn't build a business model that matched our ambition. Technical achievement without financial sustainability is a beautiful machine that runs out of fuel."
⚠️ Build revenue discipline in parallel with technical ambition. A brilliant product that can't sustain itself helps no one.
Clement Delangue
CEO, Hugging Face — built the GitHub of AI by giving everything away for free
"Our business model was counterintuitive: give away the platform, give away the models, give away the tools — then charge enterprises for the managed service, the compliance, and the support. Community is the moat. Community is the distribution. Community is the company."
🔑 Developer communities are the most durable competitive moats in software. Build them before you need them to sell.

🎓 Graduate Roadmap

Learning Roadmap to Build an LLM

A structured, opinionated sequence of resources — from linear algebra to production-grade LLM systems. Each phase lists the best books, courses, papers, and code repos.

01 Math & CS
→
02 ML Foundations
→
03 Deep Learning
→

01
Mathematics & CS Foundations
8–12 weeks · Prerequisites for everything below
📐
You can't meaningfully implement or debug a transformer without linear algebra (attention is matrix multiplication), calculus (backprop is the chain rule), and probability (language models are probability distributions). Don't skip this — it pays compound interest across every subsequent phase.
📚 Books
Mathematics for Machine Learning
Deisenroth, Faisal, Ong — Cambridge University Press (free PDF)
Covers linear algebra, multivariate calculus, and probability as used in ML. Best starting point.
Linear Algebra Done Right
Sheldon Axler — Springer
Conceptual, proof-based. Builds the intuition behind matrix operations rather than just mechanics.
Probability Theory: The Logic of Science
E.T. Jaynes — Cambridge
Deep probabilistic reasoning — critical for understanding loss functions, sampling, and uncertainty.
🎥 Courses
Linear Algebra — Gilbert Strang (MIT 18.06)
MIT OpenCourseWare · Free
The gold standard. Strang's geometric intuition for eigenvectors, SVD, and matrix factorizations is unmatched.
Essence of Linear Algebra
3Blue1Brown · YouTube · Free
Best visual intuition for vectors, transformations, and eigendecomposition. Watch before or alongside Strang.
Statistics 110: Probability
Joe Blitzstein, Harvard · YouTube · Free
Rigorous probability with excellent examples. Covers distributions, Bayes, conditional probability.
💻 Code Practice
numpy: Linear Algebra from Scratch
numpy.org docs + exercises
Implement matrix multiply, SVD, eigendecomposition, softmax from scratch in NumPy before using PyTorch.
The Matrix Calculus You Need for Deep Learning
Parr & Howard · arXiv:1802.01528
The single best reference for Jacobians and the chain rule as used in backpropagation. Bookmark permanently.
02
Machine Learning Foundations
6–10 weeks · Classical ML before deep learning
🧮
Understanding gradient descent, regularization, generalization theory, and the bias-variance tradeoff builds the mental model that makes deep learning concepts obvious rather than mysterious. LLM researchers who skipped this phase struggle to diagnose training failures.
📚 Books
Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning
Christopher Bishop — Springer (free PDF)
The definitive Bayesian ML textbook. Probability distributions, graphical models, and variational inference all appear later in LLM work.
The Elements of Statistical Learning
Hastie, Tibshirani, Friedman — Stanford (free PDF)
Rigorous treatment of statistical theory behind ML. Regularization, ensemble methods, cross-validation.
🎥 Courses
CS229: Machine Learning
Andrew Ng, Stanford · Coursera or YouTube · Free audit
The foundational ML course. Linear models, SVMs, neural nets, EM algorithm. Still the best structured intro.
Practical Deep Learning for Coders
fast.ai · fast.ai/courses · Free
Top-down approach — train models first, then understand why. Excellent complement to bottom-up courses.
💻 Projects
Implement linear regression, logistic regression, and MLP in pure NumPy
Self-project · ~2 weeks
The backprop implementation in NumPy is the best preparation for understanding PyTorch autograd internals.
sklearn documentation + source code
scikit-learn.org
Reading sklearn source reveals how professional ML code is structured: fit/transform APIs, pipelines, cross-validation.
03
Deep Learning — From Backprop to CNNs
6–8 weeks · Neural network fundamentals and PyTorch mastery
🧠
Deep learning is the substrate on which LLMs run. You need fluency with PyTorch, understand initialization, normalization, and activation functions, and be able to implement and debug custom neural network layers. CNNs and RNNs illuminate the design choices that made transformers necessary.
📚 Books
Deep Learning
Goodfellow, Bengio, Courville — MIT Press (free online)
The canonical textbook. Chapter 6 (MLPs), Chapter 8 (optimization), Chapter 9 (CNNs) are essential reads.
Dive into Deep Learning (d2l.ai)
Aston Zhang et al. — d2l.ai · Free interactive book
Best hands-on deep learning book with runnable code in every chapter. Covers everything from linear models to attention.
🎥 Courses
Neural Networks: Zero to Hero
Andrej Karpathy · YouTube · Free
Builds a GPT from scratch starting from backprop. The single best course for LLM builders. Do every exercise.
Deep Learning Specialization
Andrew Ng · Coursera · ~$50/month
Thorough coverage of deep learning concepts with structured assignments. Excellent for systematic learners.
CS231n: CNNs for Visual Recognition
Stanford · cs231n.stanford.edu · Free
The backprop assignments are legendary. Assignment 2 (BatchNorm, Dropout) builds intuition crucial for LLMs.
💻 Code
micrograd
github.com/karpathy/micrograd
237-line autograd engine. Implementing this gives complete understanding of how PyTorch/JAX compute gradients.
PyTorch Official Tutorials
pytorch.org/tutorials
Learn custom Dataset, DataLoader, nn.Module, autograd, and the training loop pattern used in every LLM codebase.
04
NLP Fundamentals & The Transformer
4–6 weeks · From word embeddings to self-attention
📝
Word2Vec, GloVe, RNNs, and seq2seq are not just historical curiosities — they explain why transformers were designed the way they were. Reading the original "Attention Is All You Need" paper after understanding RNNs reveals each design choice as a specific solution to a specific limitation.
📚 Books & Guides
Speech and Language Processing (3rd ed.)
Jurafsky & Martin · web.stanford.edu/~jurafsky/slp3 · Free draft
The NLP bible. Tokenization, n-grams, language models, neural NLP — comprehensive and freely updated.
Natural Language Processing with Transformers
Tunstall, von Werra, Wolf — O'Reilly (HuggingFace book)
Practical guide to using HuggingFace transformers. Best bridge from theory to working code.
📄 Foundational Papers
Attention Is All You Need
Vaswani et al. (2017) · arXiv:1706.03762
The paper that started everything. Read it 3 times — once for the idea, once for the math, once for the implementation details.
BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers
Devlin et al. (2018) · arXiv:1810.04805
MLM pre-training and the encoder-only paradigm. Essential for understanding what GPT improved on.
Language Models are Few-Shot Learners (GPT-3)
Brown et al. (2020) · arXiv:2005.14165
Defines in-context learning, few-shot prompting, and scaling laws. The paper that made LLMs mainstream.
🎥 Courses
CS224N: NLP with Deep Learning
Stanford · cs224n.stanford.edu · Free videos + assignments
The definitive NLP course. Covers word vectors, RNNs, attention, and transformers with rigorous assignments.
The Illustrated Transformer
Jay Alammar · jalammar.github.io · Free
The best visual walkthrough of multi-head attention, positional encoding, and the encoder-decoder stack.
05
LLM Architecture Deep Dive
4–6 weeks · GPT internals, tokenizers, and modern variants
🏗️
Reading papers and watching lectures about transformers is not the same as implementing one from scratch. This phase is about building a GPT that trains, understanding every hyperparameter, and tracing every forward pass from token IDs to logits. Karpathy's nanoGPT is the right vehicle.
💻 Essential Repos
nanoGPT
github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT
~300 lines of PyTorch implementing a complete GPT. Train on Shakespeare. Read every line. The best LLM learning artifact that exists.
llm.c
github.com/karpathy/llm.c
GPT-2 training in pure C/CUDA. Reading this teaches you what PyTorch abstracts away — memory layout, CUDA kernels, attention math.
litgpt
github.com/Lightning-AI/litgpt
Production-quality implementations of LLaMA, Gemma, Mistral, Phi. Study the config system and model variants.
📄 Architecture Papers
LLaMA: Open and Efficient Foundation LMs
Touvron et al. (2023) · arXiv:2302.13971
RoPE, SwiGLU, RMSNorm — the modern transformer recipe. Every open LLM since uses these components.
FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Attention
Dao et al. (2022) · arXiv:2205.14135
Tiling-based IO-aware attention. Understanding this is necessary for anyone training or serving LLMs.
Mixtral of Experts
Jiang et al. (2024) · arXiv:2401.04088
Sparse MoE architecture that matches dense 70B performance at 13B active parameters. The frontier architecture.
Tiktoken / SentencePiece internals
github.com/openai/tiktoken + google/sentencepiece
Implement BPE from scratch — tokenizer choice affects model vocabulary size, multilingual capability, and training efficiency.
🎥 Deep Dives
Let's build GPT — from scratch, in code
Andrej Karpathy · YouTube · Free
2-hour video building nanoGPT live. Watch it twice — once following along, once reading the repo source.
LLM Visualization
bbycroft.net/llm · Free interactive tool
Animated, interactive walkthrough of every step in GPT-2's forward pass. Invaluable for visual learners.
06
Pre-training & Training at Scale
4–6 weeks · Data pipelines, distributed training, and compute
⚡
Training a GPT-2-size model on a single GPU is very different from training a 70B model on 1,000 GPUs. This phase covers the systems engineering of distributed training — data parallelism, model parallelism, gradient checkpointing, and how scaling laws should drive your architecture decisions.
📄 Must-Read Papers
Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models
Kaplan et al., OpenAI (2020) · arXiv:2001.08361
The original scaling laws. Power-law relationships between compute, data, and model size. Foundation for all training budget decisions.
Training Compute-Optimal LLMs (Chinchilla)
Hoffmann et al., DeepMind (2022) · arXiv:2203.15556
Revised scaling laws showing models were undertrained. Changed how every lab allocates compute. Essential reading.
Megatron-LM: Training Multi-Billion Parameter LMs
Shoeybi et al., NVIDIA (2019) · arXiv:1909.08053
Tensor parallelism for transformers. How to split a transformer layer across multiple GPUs.
The Pile: An 800GB Dataset of Diverse Text
Gao et al., EleutherAI (2020) · arXiv:2101.00027
Data diversity matters. The Pile showed that domain mixture dramatically affects downstream task performance.
💻 Tools & Repos
Megatron-LM
github.com/NVIDIA/Megatron-LM
The production framework behind GPT-3, Turing-NLG, and most NVIDIA-trained models. Study the parallelism configs.
DeepSpeed
github.com/microsoft/DeepSpeed
ZeRO optimizer reduces memory footprint by 8x. Used in almost every large-scale training run. Understand ZeRO-1/2/3.
Datatrove
github.com/huggingface/datatrove
HuggingFace's data pipeline for LLM pre-training. Dedup, quality filtering, format conversion at petabyte scale.
Weights & Biases (wandb)
wandb.ai · Free tier available
Essential for tracking loss curves, gradient norms, and learning rate schedules across training runs. Industry standard.
🎥 Courses & Guides
PyTorch Distributed Training Guide
pytorch.org/tutorials/distributed · Free
DDP, FSDP, pipeline parallelism — official tutorials with working code. Start with DDP before moving to FSDP.
Hugging Face Course — Chapter on Training
huggingface.co/learn · Free
Accelerate library, mixed precision, gradient checkpointing. Bridges academic concepts with practical HuggingFace tooling.
07
Fine-tuning, RLHF & Alignment
4–6 weeks · Instruction tuning, preference learning, and safety
🎯
A pre-trained LLM is a next-token predictor, not an assistant. Fine-tuning, RLHF, and alignment techniques transform a raw language model into something useful and safe. This is where the difference between GPT-2 and ChatGPT lives — and where most applied LLM work happens today.
📄 Key Papers
Training Language Models to Follow Instructions (InstructGPT)
Ouyang et al., OpenAI (2022) · arXiv:2203.02155
The RLHF paper. SFT → reward model → PPO fine-tuning. The blueprint for ChatGPT and every instruction-tuned model.
Direct Preference Optimization (DPO)
Rafailov et al. (2023) · arXiv:2305.18290
Eliminates the reward model and PPO — aligns with preferences using simple classification loss. Now the most widely used alignment technique.
Constitutional AI: Harmlessness from AI Feedback
Bai et al., Anthropic (2022) · arXiv:2212.08073
RLAIF — using AI feedback instead of human labels. Scalable alignment that doesn't require labeler armies.
LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models
Hu et al. (2021) · arXiv:2106.09685
Fine-tune a 7B model on one GPU by freezing weights and training low-rank adapter matrices. Essential for applied work.
💻 Tools
TRL (Transformer Reinforcement Learning)
github.com/huggingface/trl
HuggingFace's library for SFT, reward modeling, PPO, and DPO. The standard toolkit for alignment work.
Axolotl
github.com/axolotl-ai-cloud/axolotl
Config-driven fine-tuning — LoRA, QLoRA, full fine-tune with one YAML file. Used extensively in the open-source community.
OpenRLHF
github.com/OpenRLHF/OpenRLHF
Open-source PPO, GRPO, and DPO training framework designed for large-scale RLHF. Study the reward modeling pipeline.
🎥 Courses
RLHF: From PPO to DPO
Hugging Face Blog series · huggingface.co/blog · Free
Step-by-step blog posts on reward modeling, PPO training, and DPO with working code. Best practical reference.
CS324: Large Language Models
Stanford · stanford-cs324.github.io · Free
Stanford's LLM course covering alignment, safety, and evaluation alongside architecture and training.
08
Deployment, Inference & Production
3–5 weeks · Serving LLMs efficiently at scale
🚀
A trained model sitting on a disk generates no value. Deployment requires understanding quantization (4-bit inference on consumer hardware), continuous batching (vLLM's PagedAttention), speculative decoding, and how to build API layers that handle thousands of concurrent requests economically.
📄 Key Papers
Efficient Memory Management for LLM Serving (vLLM)
Kwon et al. (2023) · arXiv:2309.06180
PagedAttention — virtual memory for KV caches. The technique behind 24x throughput improvements in production LLM serving.
GPTQ: Accurate Post-Training Quantization for Generative Pre-trained Transformers
Frantar et al. (2022) · arXiv:2210.17323
Quantize a 70B model to 4-bit without significant quality loss. Enables LLaMA-70B on 2× A100s instead of 8×.
Speculative Decoding
Leviathan et al. (2022) · arXiv:2211.17192
Draft with a small model, verify with the large model. 2-3× latency reduction with zero quality loss.
💻 Production Frameworks
vLLM
github.com/vllm-project/vllm
The industry standard for LLM serving. PagedAttention, continuous batching, OpenAI-compatible API. Run this first.
llama.cpp
github.com/ggerganov/llama.cpp
Inference on CPU and Apple Silicon. GGUF quantization. Best for understanding low-level inference optimization.
TensorRT-LLM
github.com/NVIDIA/TensorRT-LLM
NVIDIA's production inference stack. Kernel fusion, int8/fp8 quantization, in-flight batching. Used by OpenAI and Anthropic.
Ollama
github.com/ollama/ollama
One-command local LLM serving. Use for rapid prototyping and testing before moving to production deployment stacks.

KV caching, quantization, and batching explained with benchmarks. Practical reference for inference engineers.

Covers the full deployment pipeline: prompting, chains, evaluation, monitoring, and infrastructure. Strong production focus.

🔬 Research Frontier

The Research Landscape

What's solved, what's open, where to focus your PhD or research career

🧩 Grand Open Problems in LLM Research

🎯
True Reasoning
Can LLMs genuinely reason, or is it sophisticated pattern matching? Failure on novel logical forms (Winogrande variants, ARC-Challenge) suggests current limits. Chain-of-thought helps but doesn't solve compositionality. Key papers: Dziri et al. 2023 "Faith and Fate", Bubeck et al. 2023 "Sparks of AGI".
Status: Deeply open
🔄
Continual Learning
LLMs forget old knowledge when trained on new data (catastrophic forgetting). Current solutions: replay buffers, EWC, LoRA mixing — all partial. No clean solution at scale. Active area: DARE, TIES merging, gradient projection methods.
Status: Active area
🕵️
Interpretability
We cannot explain why models produce specific outputs. Mechanistic interpretability (Anthropic's circuits work, superposition hypothesis) is making progress at toy scale. Scaling to production models is unsolved. Critical for safety and trust.
Status: Early stage
📏
Reliable Calibration
Models express false confidence. RLHF makes calibration worse (Kadavath et al. 2022). Temperature scaling helps at small scale. At deployment scale, models confidently hallucinate. Key work: "Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know".
Status: Partially solved
⚖️
Scalable Alignment
Current RLHF requires human labels that may not scale to superhuman capabilities. Debate, amplification, scalable oversight are theoretical proposals. Superalignment team at OpenAI, MIRI, ARC working on this. No solution validated at scale.
Status: Unsolved
🌐
Long-Horizon Agency
Agents that can plan and execute tasks over many steps (SWE-Bench requires 50+ steps). Current models fail on tasks requiring persistent memory, error recovery, and goal-directed planning. ReAct, Reflexion, AutoGPT are starting points, not solutions.
Status: Emerging

🏛️ Key Research Labs & Their Focus Areas

OpenAI
Scaling, RLHF, reasoning (o1/o3), multimodal, alignment
Key: GPT-4, InstructGPT, Scaling Laws, DALL-E, Whisper, Superalignment
🔒 Mostly closed; technical reports public
Anthropic
Constitutional AI, interpretability, long-context, safety
Key: Claude series, Constitutional AI, Toy Models of Superposition, Scaling Monosemanticity
🔒 Closed weights; alignment research published

Chinchilla scaling, MoE, Gemini, AlphaCode, long-context
Key: Chinchilla, Flamingo, PaLM, Gemini, AlphaCode, GraphCast
🔒 Closed; extensive publications
Meta AI (FAIR)
Open weights (LLaMA), multimodal, efficiency, world models
Key: LLaMA 1/2/3, OPT, NLLB, ImageBind, Segment Anything
✅ Open weights (LLaMA); code released

Key: LoRA, Alpaca, DPO, HELM, FlashAttention, vLLM, Mistral collaboration
